targets.problem: In the constant-rate CSF infusion test, resistance to outflow (R_out) is recovered reliably but CEREBROSPINAL COMPLIANCE/ELASTANCE is not: compliance parameters 'agreed poorly between methods (R2 = 0.3-0.7) and varied considerably within the observed infusion periods', while R_out converged to within +/-10% in 10-15 min. The specific stuck sub-question: is the poor identifiability of compliance an intrinsic property of the physiology, or an artifact of fitting a plateau-approach model to a transient in which the measurement system's own storage and the pressure-dependence of compliance are not separated -- and do the diagnostic tools built for exactly this identifiability problem in subsurface pressure-transient testing (log-log pressure-derivative diagnostic plots, explicit instrument-storage models, rate-history deconvolution, pseudopressure transforms for stress-sensitive storage) recover compliance from infusion traces that current plateau/ODE fitting cannot?
targets.notes:
The two fields are solving the same inverse problem with different words. A constant-rate CSF infusion is a constant-rate injection test into a compliant, leaky compartment with a fixed outflow conductance and an instrument (catheter + transducer + tubing) that has its own compliance in series. The subsurface well-test literature calls the identical quantities STORATIVITY (= compliance), TRANSMISSIVITY/PERMEABILITY (= 1/R_out), WELLBORE STORAGE (= catheter/system compliance, which dominates exactly the early-time window where compliance information lives), and STRESS-SENSITIVE / PRESSURE-DEPENDENT STORAGE (= the elastance term E that makes compliance fall as ICP rises). That field spent 1950-2005 on the specific failure mode the CSF literature now reports: early-time storage and late-time conductance are strongly correlated in a single constant-rate test, so naive curve-fitting trades one off against the other and the storage estimate is the one that goes unstable. Their answers were (a) Bourdet's log-log pressure-derivative diagnostic plot (1983), which makes the storage-dominated and conductance-dominated regimes visually separable and tells you which part of the trace may legitimately be fitted for which parameter; (b) explicit deconvolution of the instrument/storage response (von Schroeter & Levitan, early 2000s) so that imperfect, non-constant and interrupted rate histories can still be inverted -- directly relevant because the CSF literature already notes 'it is not necessary that the ICP reaches a plateau'; (c) pseudopressure transforms that linearize a system whose storage depends on pressure.

MECHANISTIC REASON THE GAP IS REAL: vocabulary non-overlap in both directions, plus a disciplinary firewall (petroleum/hydrogeology journals vs neurosurgery journals, no shared indexing terms). Nothing in the clinical phrase 'cerebrospinal compliance' retrieves 'storativity', and a derivative-diagnostic paper about a well does not index on 'hydrocephalus'. The CSF field independently rediscovered the physics as poroelasticity (which IS cited in brain modelling), but poroelastic FORWARD simulation is a different tool from well-test INVERSE diagnostics -- a poroelastic infusion-test simulation paper concludes that with arterial pulsations plus nonlinear compliance 'solutions have to be interpreted very carefully to predict parameter values', which is a statement of the identifiability problem, not a method for it.

What the comb should look for: Bourdet/Gringarten derivative-diagnostic methodology; Agarwal-Al-Hussainy-Ramey and the wellbore-storage deconvolution line; the groundwater slug-test and leaky-aquifer (Hantush-Jacob) analogues, which are closer to CSF scale than oilfield cases; and specifically the well-test literature's own quantitative statements about HOW MUCH of the early-time trace must be free of instrument storage before storativity is identifiable -- that number translates directly into a design constraint on infusion-test catheters and sampling rate.

CHEAP VERIFICATION (physical coherence checked): purely retrospective and computational. Take existing archived constant-rate infusion-test pressure traces (the Cambridge/Umea computerised infusion datasets are the obvious source; the Czosnyka computerised method is the incumbent comparator), and (1) replot each as a log-log pressure-derivative diagnostic, (2) test whether the derivative plot separates an early instrument/compartment-storage regime from a later outflow-dominated regime, (3) refit compliance using only the window the diagnostic licenses, plus a deconvolution of the known catheter/transducer compliance, and (4) ask whether between-method agreement for compliance improves on the published R2 = 0.3-0.7 benchmark while R_out estimates stay unchanged (the latter is the negative control -- if R_out moves, the reanalysis is wrong). Physical coherence: the analogy requires only linear-in-the-small storage plus conductance plus a series instrument capacitance, all of which demonstrably exist in the CSF infusion setup; and where the CSF system is nonlinear (compliance falling with pressure above a reference), the well-test toolkit's own pseudopressure/stress-sensitive machinery is the designated tool rather than an assumption being violated. The one real mismatch to state up front: the CSF trace carries large arterial and respiratory pulsations that have no well-test counterpart, so a derivative plot must be computed on a low-pass-filtered trace, and that filtering choice is itself a parameter that has to be reported.

targets.problem: Zero-heat-flux (ZHF) cutaneous thermometry is accurate at thermal steady state but fails during exactly the episodes that matter: on cardiopulmonary bypass, ZHF-vs-nasopharyngeal limits of agreement 'exceeded the clinically acceptable +/- 0.5 degC during CPB-cooling and CPB-rewarming, reaching up to +/- 2.3 degC', with ZHF tracking a visibly slower rate of change than the reference. The specific stuck sub-question: is that transient error a fixed, identifiable dynamic response of the sensor-plus-skin system -- and therefore invertible offline from the ZHF trace alone by the dynamic-compensation methods built for slow heat-flux and embedded-thermocouple sensors in thermal engineering -- or is it, as the clinical literature currently asserts, irreducibly physiological?
targets.notes:
ZHF thermometry is a NULL method by construction: a servo heater drives the flux through an insulating pad to zero so the skin surface equilibrates with deep tissue, and the reading is then taken as core. Nulling is intrinsically a steady-state operation; the system's approach to null is governed by the thermal mass and conductance of pad plus skin plus perfused subcutis, so during a forced transient the output is necessarily a lagged, low-pass-filtered, amplitude-attenuated version of the true deep temperature. The clinical field treats this as a nuisance to be excluded (studies carve out cooling/rewarming phases) or as physiology. The most on-point 2026 CPB paper explicitly attributes the lag to 'physiological delays in thermal equilibration rather than limitations inherent to the zero-heat-flux technique' -- that attribution is a falsifiable claim, and it is the claim this target attacks, because a first-order or two-node lumped sensor-plus-tissue model predicts the same qualitative signature (slower rate of change, growing offset in the direction of the ramp, offset that decays after the ramp stops) with no physiology invoked at all.

The old/other corpus: thermal-engineering transient thermometry, which has treated 'my sensor is slower than the thing I am measuring' as a solved inverse problem for decades -- dynamic error correction of thermocouples and heat-flux gauges posed as an inverse heat conduction problem, embedded-thermocouple correction transfer functions (a 2005 thesis line, dynamically correcting installation-induced bias via an embedded-thermocouple correction transfer function), and the whole regularization literature for the resulting ill-posed deconvolution (Tikhonov, and more recent filtered-kernel regularization inside physics-informed networks reporting ~0.83% peak relative error vs 2.05-2.2% for older schemes). That corpus also supplies the thing the clinical field has never measured: a response time.

MECHANISTIC REASON THE GAP IS REAL: different vocabularies for the same physical quantity, plus opposite framings of the same artifact. The engineering field says 'sensor time constant / dynamic error / inverse heat conduction'; the clinical field says 'time lag for establishing temperature equilibrium' and 'isothermal tunnel formation' and then handles it STATISTICALLY -- the CPB paper's own time adjustment is 'residuals from linear regressions on time, not a physical model of sensor response'. A regression on time cannot invert a convolution, so the correction being applied is categorically the wrong class of tool for the artifact being corrected. There is also a device-design reason the gap persisted: ZHF was commercialized as a single-number display, so the raw heater power and dual-thermistor signals that a deconvolution needs are not exposed by the clinical products -- a documented-in-hardware barrier, not a scientific one.

What the comb should look for: the Gardon-gauge / thin-film heat-flux-sensor dynamic calibration corpus; inverse-heat-conduction deconvolution with regularization; embedded-thermocouple correction transfer functions and how their time constants were identified experimentally (step response in a stirred bath); and critically, whether that corpus already establishes the identifiability limits -- how much sensor noise destroys a deconvolution at a given ramp rate -- since those limits set whether a 1-2 degC/min CPB ramp is recoverable at all.

CHEAP VERIFICATION (physical coherence checked): three cheap legs, in order of cost. (1) Bench, no subjects: mount a ZHF pad on a perfused skin-equivalent phantom or a water-jacketed gel block, drive the block through step and ramp changes spanning CPB rates, and identify the sensor-plus-pad transfer function (time constant(s), DC gain). This simply measures the number the clinical literature has never reported -- the Europe PMC sweep found 'No record explicitly measures response time or lag of a ZHF sensor.' (2) Retrospective, computational: take already-published paired ZHF-vs-nasopharyngeal traces from CPB cooling/rewarming and test whether a one- or two-time-constant deconvolution with the bench-identified constants tightens the limits of agreement toward +/- 0.5 degC. Negative control: the same deconvolution must NOT degrade agreement during the thermally steady phases, where mean bias is already small (-0.55 to 0.28 degC). (3) If (1) and (2) hold, the strong test: does a ZHF trace plus deconvolution predict the direction and magnitude of the error during the rewarming ramp, where the clinical paper measured TZHF rising relative to TNP to about 0.53 degC by the end -- a signed, specific number to hit.

Physical coherence: the imported method operates on a linear(izable) lumped thermal system driven below its own bandwidth, which is precisely the ZHF regime during a slow surgical ramp, so there is no regime where the old technique cannot function. The honest constraints: the ill-posedness means noise is amplified by differentiation, so leg (2) depends on sampling rate and quantization of the archived traces (clinical monitors often log at low rates and 0.1 degC resolution -- if so, deconvolution may be infeasible on legacy data and leg (1) plus a prospective high-rate recording is required); and perfusion changes DO modulate the tissue conductance, so the transfer function is not strictly time-invariant -- the test is whether a fixed-parameter deconvolution captures enough of the artifact to matter, not whether it is exact.

SCOPE NOTE: this is an instrumentation-physics hypothesis for device researchers. It is not clinical guidance and prescribes nothing for patient management.

targets.problem: Multi-site replication projects in psychology and experimental social science (Many Labs, Registered Replication Reports) need to decide whether observed between-site spread in an effect size reflects real moderation by sample/setting or merely a few badly-behaved sites. Current practice estimates a single random-effects tau (plus I-squared) per effect, an approach known to be badly biased downward and poorly calibrated when the number of sites is ~20-60. The specific stuck sub-question: with k sites each measuring the same pre-registered protocol, how do you (a) separate within-site imprecision from between-site location shift, and (b) identify WHICH sites are discrepant in location versus in scatter, with a calibrated decision rule? Analytical chemistry and physical metrology solved exactly this problem between 1950 and 1994 and standardised the solution as ISO 5725-2 and ASTM E691: repeatability/reproducibility variance decomposition, Mandel's h statistic (per-lab location consistency) and Mandel's k statistic (per-lab scatter consistency) with tabulated critical values, Youden two-sample plots to separate systematic from random lab error, and ISO 13528 robust consensus-value estimation with z-scores. The hypothesis: porting this machinery to multi-site replication data yields per-site diagnostics and a site-outlier decision rule that the current random-effects workflow does not provide at all.
targets.notes:
CO-OCCURRENCE CHECKS RUN (bare old-method name vs bare modern problem, no field words attached):
  q1: "Mandel" "h and k statistics" replication crisis psychology -> returned two disjoint result sets: generic replication-crisis papers (Wikipedia, Gelman psych_crisis_minipaper, Frontiers 2024) and pure metrology/R-package documentation (metRology::mandel.kh, PMCMRplus::mandelhTest/mandelkTest, ASTM E691, MetricGate ISO 5725-2 docs). ZERO documents containing both.
  q2: "ISO 5725" "many labs" replication heterogeneity social science -> returned only the psychology side (Many Labs 2, Klein et al. 2018; arXiv 1710.06031; Stanley & Doucouliagos comment; HHS working paper on population/design/analytical heterogeneity). No result mentions ISO 5725.
  q3 (reverse direction, to catch the bridge being built from the metrology side): metrology interlaboratory comparison methods applied to "reproducibility crisis" psychology social science consensus value Youden plot -> again two disjoint sets. Metrology side: NIST/ITL Engineering Statistics Handbook 1.3.3.31 Youden Plot; Springer Accred. Qual. Assur. 2013 Youden-plot proficiency-testing study; JRC EURL interlab reports; arXiv 2606.06045 RADIOMAG magnetic-hyperthermia round robin (uses Youden plots -- but for a physical measurand). Social-science side: SEP 'Reproducibility of Scientific Results', Social Science Replication Project, IRSP. No crossover document.

MODERN REVIEW FETCHED AND REFERENCE LIST CHECKED: arXiv:1710.06031, 'Large Scale Replication Projects in Contemporary Psychological Research' (the most on-point methods critique of how multi-site replication projects analyse between-site variability). Result of checking its bibliography for metrology/ISO/ASTM/Mandel/Youden/measurement-science entries: "None of the references concern metrology, ISO, ASTM, Mandel, Youden, or physical/chemical measurement science." The three nearest entries are Klein et al. 2014 (Many Labs), Lindsay & Ehrenberg 1993 'The design of replicated studies', and Ehrenberg & Bound 1993 -- all psychology/statistics. What the paper proposes instead: a hierarchical multilevel model with partial pooling, I-squared with Pigott (2012) 25/50/75 percent thresholds, post-stratification (Park et al. 2004; Kennedy & Gelman 2018). It explicitly criticises the two-parameter random-effects model and the zero-heterogeneity test as "poorly calibrated when the number of laboratories is small" and cites Chung et al. (2013a,b) on downward bias -- i.e. it diagnoses precisely the problem ISO 5725-2 variance components and Mandel h/k address, and reaches for none of it.

WHY THE GAP HAS A STRUCTURAL REASON (not merely 'nobody cited it'): (1) Vocabulary split -- metrology fixes 'repeatability' and 'reproducibility' as technical terms for within- and between-laboratory precision (ISO 5725-1/-2, VIM); psychology uses 'reproducibility' and 'replicability' with the opposite-ish and contested meanings, so a keyword search from either side misses the other. (2) Publication-venue split -- the core corpus is ISO/ASTM/IUPAC standards documents and the NIST Engineering Statistics Handbook, which are paywalled standards or grey literature, NOT journal articles, so they are largely absent from citation indices that social scientists search. (3) Mandel's own papers are in Journal of Quality Technology / Materials Research & Standards, 1960s-70s, not indexed alongside psychology.

CHEAP VERIFICATION STEP -- DATASET + ESTIMATOR, BOTH NAMED AND CONFIRMED TO EXIST:
  Dataset: Many Labs 2 (Klein et al. 2018, AMPPS 1(4):443-490, doi 10.1177/2515245918810225). Public repository osf.io/8cd4r (confirmed live; its wiki documents the 28 findings and the preregistered design and carries a July 2019 correction note). A ready-made site-level extract exists on CRAN: psymetadata::manylabs2018 -- confirmed 1,414 rows, 23 variables, including a `lab` site identifier and effect sizes in both r and Cohen's d, sourced from osf.io/ux3eh. Note the raw participant-level ML2 data contains PII and is restricted, so use the aggregated site-level file. Supplementary: the Registered Replication Reports (e.g. Alogna et al. verbal overshadowing) for a second, smaller k.
  Estimator: ISO 5725-2 one-way random-effects variance decomposition into s_r (repeatability) and s_R (reproducibility), then Mandel's h (standardised between-site deviation of each site mean from the grand mean) and Mandel's k (ratio of each site's within-site SD to the pooled within-site SD), with ASTM E691 critical values. Both are implemented and installable today: PMCMRplus::mandelhTest and PMCMRplus::mandelkTest (documented as implementing ASTM E691) and metRology::mandel.kh. Add ISO 13528 robust consensus value (Algorithm A) and per-site z-scores. Because each ML2 site ran many of the 28 effects, the Youden two-sample plot applies directly with two effects per site.
  Falsifiable outcome: run Mandel h/k on each of the 28 ML2 effects and ask whether the flagged sites concentrate on particular labs across effects. If a small number of sites are flagged repeatedly across unrelated effects, that is site-level systematic error (a lab property), which the per-effect random-effects tau structurally cannot see because it is fit one effect at a time -- and it would partially undercut the ML2 headline conclusion that variability 'was attributable more to the effect being studied than to the sample or setting'. If flags are scattered at the nominal rate, the import is genuinely null and the target closes cheaply.

Searched q1, q2 and the reverse-direction q3 above. All three returned cleanly disjoint result sets; the only Youden-plot application found in a round-robin context was arXiv 2606.06045, a magnetic-hyperthermia physics study, not social science. Caveat recorded honestly: absence of search hits is weaker evidence than a reference-list check, which is why the reference-list check below was also done.

CLAIM: 'The authoritative modern methods review of multi-site replication variability does not cite the metrology corpus.' VERIFIED BY FETCHING AND READING THE REFERENCE LIST of arXiv:1710.06031. Quoted result: 'None of the references concern metrology, ISO, ASTM, Mandel, Youden, or physical/chemical measurement science.' This is the specific check that 18 of 27 prior targets failed, and it passed here.

CLAIM: 'Current practice relies on per-effect random-effects tau / I-squared and is known to be badly calibrated at small k.' VERIFIED, and verified from the modern side rather than asserted: arXiv:1710.06031 itself says standard heterogeneity estimators are biased downwards and that zero-heterogeneity estimates 'result implausibly often when the number of labs is small', and recommends hierarchical partial pooling plus I-squared instead. So the problem is live and self-described, not invented here.

CLAIM: 'The dataset exists and is usable without special access.' VERIFIED. osf.io/8cd4r confirmed live as the ML2 repository; CRAN package psymetadata exposes dataset manylabs2018 with a confirmed 1,414 rows x 23 variables including a lab identifier and both r and d effect sizes. ALSO verified the limitation: raw participant-level ML2 data contains PII and is not fully public, so the check must run on site-level aggregates -- which is exactly what Mandel h needs (site means + n), though Mandel k additionally needs per-site within-cell SDs; if the aggregated file lacks SDs, Mandel k must be computed from the OSF per-site summary files rather than the CRAN extract. FLAGGED AS PARTIALLY UNVERIFIED: I did not open the OSF file tree to confirm that per-site within-cell SDs are present. The combing agent should check this FIRST, because Mandel k is half the method.

CLAIM: 'The estimator is implemented and runnable.' VERIFIED. PMCMRplus::mandelhTest and ::mandelkTest (documented against ASTM E691) and metRology::mandel.kh all confirmed present in current CRAN documentation; NIST Engineering Statistics Handbook section 1.3.3.31 documents the Youden plot construction and interpretation.

targets.problem: The 2020 US Census was released through a differentially private TopDown Algorithm whose post-processing (non-negativity, hierarchical consistency, invariant state totals) is known to inject bias, especially for small geographies and detailed age/race cells, damaging the small-area demographic estimates that redistricting, public-health rate denominators and school/transit planning depend on. Since 2023 the Census Bureau has released the pre-post-processing Noisy Measurement File, so users can in principle do their own, better-behaved reconstruction. The specific stuck sub-question: what is the right estimator for recovering a smooth demographic surface (e.g. single-year-of-age counts by small geography) from noisy integer counts whose measurement-error variance is KNOWN by construction, subject to known hard margins? The current state of the art in this literature is the P-spline / TOPALS family borrowed from modern smoothing (Eilers & Marx 1996). The old corpus proposed as the answer: actuarial and demographic GRADUATION theory, 1920s-1960s -- Whittaker (1923), Henderson's Whittaker-Henderson graduation types A and B, Greville, and the associated mortality-graduation literature. Whittaker-Henderson is precisely penalised least squares in which the fit term is weighted by the KNOWN measurement-error variance of each observed count and the penalty is a difference operator of chosen order, with a century of worked theory on choosing the penalty order, handling hard end constraints and reproducing known totals exactly. That is a structurally exact match to the DP case, where sigma-squared is not a nuisance parameter to be guessed but a published design constant.
targets.notes:
CO-OCCURRENCE CHECK RUN (bare old-method name vs bare modern problem, no field words):
  q1: "Whittaker-Henderson" graduation differential privacy census -> ZERO documents containing both. Results were entirely the modern side: Garfinkel/Abowd-adjacent DP-census papers, arXiv 2410.09296 on the realised privacy guarantees, the Census Bureau TopDown/DAS documentation, the Georgetown and WJLTA policy pieces, and 'Differential privacy of hierarchical Census data: An optimization approach'. No result mentions graduation, Whittaker or Henderson.
  q2: post-processing differential privacy census noisy measurement file smoothing demographic counts estimator -> surfaced the single most on-point modern paper (see below) plus McCartan, Simko & Imai 'Making Differential Privacy Work for Census Data Users' (arXiv 2305.07208) and the Census NMF release pages. Again no graduation vocabulary anywhere.

MOST ON-POINT MODERN PAPER FETCHED AND REFERENCE LIST CHECKED: 'Reconstruction of age distributions from differentially private census data' (PMC9596350). This is the closest existing attempt at exactly the proposed task. Findings, quoted/confirmed from the fetched text:
  - Method used: P-TOPALS (Dyrting 2020), a penalised B-spline with an external prior, N_x = Nhat_x * exp(B_x . theta), theta by penalised log-likelihood penalising first differences of adjacent spline weights, roughness lambda chosen by BIC, solved by iterated linear regressions. Under the assumption that 'the noise injected by TDA can be approximated by a normal distribution' the likelihood is weighted by 1/sigma-squared -- i.e. the paper has ALREADY arrived at the Whittaker-Henderson functional form by a different route, which strengthens rather than weakens the lead.
  - Reference-list check for the old corpus: 'The bibliography does not cite Whittaker, Henderson, Greville, Hoem, or any work described as graduation.' Its smoothing ancestry is Eilers & Marx (1996), Currie et al. (2004), de Beer (2011, 2012), plus Arriaga (1968) and United Nations (1956) for age-misreporting, and Schwarz (1978) for BIC. So the 1923-1960 graduation corpus is genuinely unread here.
  - AND the paper names its own binding defect, which is exactly what the old corpus fixes: 'As a proxy for the variance parameter sigma-squared, we used the mean square difference between DP and SF age distributions' -- i.e. it estimated the noise variance by differencing against the published 2010 SF1 counts, which the authors concede is unavailable in a production setting, and they call on the Census Bureau to release sigma-squared. Graduation theory is built for the case where the weight 1/sigma-squared is KNOWN a priori; and since 2023 the Noisy Measurement File plus the published production privacy-loss-budget allocation make it known. The lead is therefore not 'apply an old method' but 'the old method's defining assumption became true in 2023 and nobody re-opened the question'.

WHY THE GAP HAS A STRUCTURAL REASON: (1) Discipline boundary -- graduation lives in actuarial science (Institute of Actuaries, Transactions of the Actuarial Society of America, actuarial exam syllabi) and the DP-census problem lives in computer science and official statistics; the two have almost no shared venues. (2) Vocabulary split -- 'graduation' is an actuarial term of art for smoothing noisy rates and means nothing in CS; a CS author searching 'smoothing' or 'regularisation' will never retrieve it. (3) Partly non-digitised corpus -- Henderson's and Greville's expositions are in pre-1960 actuarial society transactions and textbooks, not in modern indexed journals. Note the one honest qualification: Whittaker is acknowledged as an ancestor of P-splines inside the smoothing literature generally (Eilers has said so), so the claim here is deliberately narrow and is about the DP-census application, not about the spline literature as a whole.

CHEAP VERIFICATION STEP -- DATASET + ESTIMATOR, BOTH NAMED AND CONFIRMED TO EXIST:
  Dataset (confirmed): 2010 Census Production Settings Demographic and Housing Characteristics (DHC) Demonstration Noisy Measurement File, and the P.L. 94-171 Redistricting Demonstration NMF -- ICPSR study 38777, version V2 dated 2023-11-10, DOI 10.3886/ICPSR38777.v2 (use V2; V1 of 2023-04-03 is marked unpublished). Mirrored as an AWS Open Data registry dataset (registry.opendata.aws/census-2010-pl94-nmf and .../census-2010-dhc-nmf). Noise mechanism confirmed in the ICPSR record: zero-concentrated DP via the discrete Gaussian mechanism (Canonne et al. 2023), integer-valued noise added to each count, generated under the final production privacy-loss-budget allocation. McCartan, Simko & Imai (arXiv 2305.07208) supply a tidied, usable conversion of the NMF, which removes the main practical obstacle (they note the native release format 'is difficult to access and work with'). Benchmark truth: the published 2010 SF1 counts, which exist for the same geographies because these are DEMONSTRATION data run on 2010 inputs -- so the check has a real gold standard, unlike the 2020 production case.
  Estimator: Whittaker-Henderson graduation, type B, u_x = argmin sum_x w_x (u_x - y_x)^2 + lambda sum_x (Delta^z u_x)^2, with w_x = 1/sigma-squared_x taken from the discrete-Gaussian variance implied by the per-query production PLB allocation (documented in Abowd et al. 2022 and the DAS_2020_Redistricting_Production_Code repository) rather than estimated by differencing; difference order z = 2 and 3; plus linear equality constraints to reproduce the invariant state totals exactly. Compare, on mean squared error against SF1, against (a) the Bureau's own post-processed TopDown published tables and (b) the P-TOPALS estimates of PMC9596350.
  Falsifiable outcome: if Whittaker-Henderson with KNOWN weights does not beat P-TOPALS with proxy weights on SF1 benchmark MSE, the lead dies in one afternoon. KNOWN RISK, STATED: the per-query sigma-squared must actually be recoverable from the published PLB allocation; the ICPSR landing page does NOT tabulate per-geography-level variances and points to Abowd et al. (2022) and the production code repo instead. See premises_verified.

The ICPSR record states the file was produced under the final production PLB allocation and names the discrete Gaussian mechanism, but it does NOT tabulate the variance or SD per geographic level or per query; it points to Abowd et al. (2022) and the DAS_2020_Redistricting_Production_Code repository. I did not open Abowd et al. (2022) or the production code to confirm the per-query budget split is actually published at the granularity needed. THIS IS THE LOAD-BEARING UNVERIFIED PREMISE OF THE TARGET and the combing agent must check it before anything else: if the per-query sigma-squared is not recoverable, the target reduces to 'use a slightly different penalty than P-TOPALS' and should be killed. One mitigating note in the target's favour: the NMF reportedly contains the noisy measurements themselves, so for repeated/redundant queries the noise scale may be estimable from the file's own internal inconsistencies even if the budget split were opaque -- but that fallback is my inference and is also UNVERIFIED.

CLAIM (deliberately NOT made): 'Whittaker-Henderson is unknown to modern smoothing.' NOT CLAIMED, because it is false -- Whittaker is a recognised ancestor of P-splines within the smoothing literature. The target's claim is restricted to the DP-census reconstruction application, where the reference-list check above shows it is absent.

targets.problem: Phytophthora ramorum and P. cinnamomi root/stem diseases in forests and nurseries have no field-scale control beyond sanitation and phosphite, and phosphite is a growth suppressant rather than a cure. The stuck sub-question: is there a documented soil condition or microbial consortium that suppresses Phytophthora root rot durably in the field, with a measured mechanism, that modern forest pathology has not tested on these two species?
targets.notes: B-terms: soil suppressiveness, calcium and ammonium nitrogen effects on sporangium formation, zoospore chemotaxis and encystment, antagonistic actinomycetes, mycorrhizal exclusion, soil water potential thresholds for sporangium production. OLD VOCABULARY: 'avocado root rot' (Phytophthora cinnamomi was THE avocado problem in Australia, California and Israel 1940-1985, with a very large applied literature), 'Ashburner method' (the Australian grower-developed mulch-plus-gypsum-plus-calcium system that suppressed avocado root rot in the field before anyone could explain it), 'suppressive soils', 'damping off', 'Queensland and Western Australian jarrah dieback' forestry reports, 'Pythium and Phytophthora in nursery beds', pre-1985 Phytopathology and Australian Journal of Agricultural Research. ADJACENT NON-CITING FIELDS: horticultural extension literature, Dutch and Israeli glasshouse substrate science, and the banana/pineapple plantation pathology literature. TRAP: phosphite and Trichoderma biocontrol are both crowded modern fields; a lead must be a specific pre-1985 soil-chemical or cultural condition with a measured mechanism, and must be checked against the modern P. ramorum literature before being carried forward. || RUN-LESSONS CARRIED FORWARD (2026-10-20, 0 survivors in 6 of 9 batches): (1) An author-name string search is NOT a co-occurrence check -- search the MECHANISM in the target field's own modern vocabulary; two leads died this way. targets.problem: Electric-vehicle and industrial drive motors suffer bearing fluting and premature failure from common-mode shaft currents produced by fast-switching inverters, and SiC/GaN devices with sub-100 ns edges have made it worse. Mitigation is a grab bag (shaft grounding rings, insulated bearings, common-mode chokes, ceramic rolling elements) with no accepted design criterion predicting which machine-plus-drive combination will discharge. Specifically: a predictive criterion for electric discharge machining in the bearing film as a function of switching edge rate, bearing geometry, lubricant and speed.
targets.notes: B-terms: common-mode voltage and shaft voltage ratio, electrohydrodynamic lubricant film thickness and its breakdown strength, capacitive versus resistive bearing impedance regimes, dv/dt-driven displacement current, rotor-to-frame capacitance network. OLD VOCABULARY: 'shaft currents in electrical machinery' (a named problem since Alger and Samson's 1924 AIEE paper, with decades of turbogenerator and marine-drive literature on magnetic dissymmetry, shaft voltage and insulated pedestals), 'bearing fluting' and 'frosting', 'electrical pitting of bearings', 'homopolar flux', 'journal insulation', 'collector brush shaft grounding'. ADJACENT NON-CITING FIELDS: the tribology and lubrication-science literature on electrical breakdown of EHD oil films (a measured, modelled quantity with its own pre-1985 corpus on film thickness and dielectric strength), railway traction-motor maintenance practice, and the electrical-discharge-machining process literature, which characterised exactly the spark-erosion mechanism that damages the raceway. targets.problem: Permafrost carbon models predict thaw almost entirely by vertical heat conduction, yet observations show abrupt thaw, talik formation and thermokarst developing far faster than conduction allows, with groundwater advection and latent heat of infiltrating water implicated but not parameterised. The stuck sub-question: what is the quantitative contribution of advective heat transport by infiltrating and laterally moving water to talik development, and does an older engineering literature already contain the measurements and design formulas?
targets.notes: B-terms: advective versus conductive heat flux in a thawing active layer, latent heat of the freeze-thaw front, Stefan-problem solutions with a moving fluid, thermal conductivity of saturated versus drained organic soils, talik closure criteria. targets.problem: Post-harvest insect loss in smallholder grain storage remains large, phosphine resistance in Rhizopertha, Tribolium and Sitophilus is now widespread and in places near-complete, and no new fumigant has been registered for decades. The stuck sub-question: which non-chemical storage atmosphere or physical treatment has a documented, quantitative mortality dose-response good enough to replace phosphine at smallholder scale, and does that data already exist in an old or non-English literature?
targets.notes: B-terms: modified and controlled atmospheres (low oxygen, elevated carbon dioxide), hermetic sealing and insect respiration-driven oxygen depletion, desiccant and inert dust action on insect cuticle, thermal disinfestation kinetics, humidity thresholds for insect development. OLD VOCABULARY: 'airtight storage of grain' and 'sealed storage' (a large 1940s-70s literature from Australia CSIRO, Israel, India and the FAO), 'underground pit storage' (a very old practice studied quantitatively in Cyprus, Turkey, Argentina and the Sahel), 'inert dusts' and 'diatomaceous earth' pre-1985, 'grain cooling / aeration', 'controlled atmosphere disinfestation', 'mortality of stored-product insects in nitrogen'. ADJACENT NON-CITING FIELDS: museum and herbarium pest control (anoxia treatment has its own well-measured literature), the modified-atmosphere packaging and food-science corpus, and military/strategic grain-reserve engineering reports. TRAP: hermetic bags (PICS and similar) are a large, well-funded modern program and are NOT a find; the differentiated seam is a quantitative dose-response (exposure time, temperature, oxygen concentration, species, life stage) from the old controlled-atmosphere or pit-storage corpus that modern smallholder work has not used, or a physical treatment never re-tested. Check the FAO and CSIRO grey literature before claiming novelty. || RUN-LESSONS CARRIED FORWARD (2026-10-20, 0 survivors in 6 of 9 batches): (1) An author-name string search is NOT a co-occurrence check -- search the MECHANISM in the target field's own modern vocabulary; two leads died this way. (2) Read the scout's own cited source adversarially: in 9 of this run's refuted leads the cited source itself contradicted the lead. (3) Check the species and the study design before calling something human data. (4) If the old method and the modern method both reduce to the same estimator or the same physics under different names, that is a KILL, not a find. (5) Verify any claimed omission against the actual reference list or data file, not a search result.

targets.problem: Use the 1962–1972 SST-era hot-salt stress-corrosion-cracking (HSSCC) corpus on titanium to predict, and then test, HSSCC of gamma-TiAl (Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb class) in the 300–500 °C / solid-NaCl-deposit / moist-air window. The old corpus established (a) susceptibility rising with Al content and with ordered alpha2-Ti3Al, and (b) the mechanism as pyrohydrolytic HCl generation from chloride + water vapour between ~260–400 °C with atomic hydrogen as the embrittling species. gamma-TiAl is the highest-Al titanium material ever put into service (LPT blades, since ~2011) and has never been tested under stress in that window.
targets.notes:
B-terms / old vocabulary to search: 'hot-salt stress corrosion', 'salt cracking' (Soviet usage, Prot. Met. / Sov. Mater. Sci.), 'stress-sorption', 'pyrohydrolysis', 'anhydrous HCl + titanium', 'hydrogen halide', 'duplex anneal', 'blue spot', 'Ti-8Al-1Mo-1V', 'alpha2 / Ti3Al ordered precipitate'. Literatures to dig: NASA NTRS (Langley 1962–1972 Heimerl & Royster programme; Gray TN D-6498; Garfinkle TN D-6779), Savannah River / DuPont reports DP(NASA)-1005 and -1179 and NASA CR-1133/CR-1915 (Ondrejcin, Louthan, Rideout), ASTM STP 397 (1966, paywalled — get via library), Petersen's 1971 J. Metals review, DTIC AD0810744, and the Russian thread (Plekhanova 1976; Travkin 1979) for the thermodynamic analysis of the salt reactions. Traps to avoid: (1) do NOT write that modern HSSCC work ignores the 1960s corpus — it cites it heavily; the claim is specifically that the aluminide alloy class was never entered into the matrix. (2) Do not conflate hot corrosion (metal loss, >700 °C) with HSSCC (hydrogen-assisted cracking, 250–500 °C); a mass-change-flat result is not a no-cracking result. (3) AgCl was used as a surrogate salt in one modern study — do not read AgCl thresholds as NaCl thresholds. (4) Check whether any coating-development paper on TiAl incidentally stress-loaded at 400–500 °C before asserting novelty, and check Chinese-language journals (BUAA/NWPU groups) which dominate current TiAl salt work. || PREMISES VERIFIED AT GENERATION: I did NOT claim the literatures are disconnected, and checked that first: I pulled the full reference list of arXiv:1802.06045 (Joseph/Dye et al., HSSCC mechanisms in Ti-6246) and it cites the old corpus by name — Ondrejcin & Louthan, 'Role of Hydrogen Chloride in Hot-Salt Stress Corrosion Cracking of Titanium-Aluminium Alloys', NASA CR-1133 (1968); Ondrejcin, NASA CR-1915 (1971); H. R. Web search for gamma-TiAl HSSCC at 400–500 °C returned only molten-salt hot corrosion: Ti-48Al-2Nb-0.7Cr-0.3Si in Na2SO4+25 wt% NaCl at 900 °C; Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb at 800 °C (corrosion initiating at lamellar interfaces, alpha2 attacked preferentially — which is corroborating evidence for the mechanism, not a cracking test); Ti-46Al-8Nb at 700/800/900 °C. Pyrohydrolysis of NaCl to HCl requires water vapour and ~260 °C+, so 350/450/500 °C with a 1–3 mg/cm2 NaCl deposit in moist lab air sits inside the documented reactive window. targets.problem: Recover per-foot, per-season measured soil moisture profiles for the US Great Plains covering 1906–1940 — i.e. spanning the Dust Bowl — from the USDA Office of Dry-Land Agriculture Investigations station corpus, convert them to volumetric soil moisture, and use them as the first *observational* evaluation of 1930s soil-moisture reconstructions and of the land-surface feedbacks (vegetation loss, dust) that current Dust Bowl attribution rests on. The station network ran continuously from 1906 at, at minimum: North Platte NE, Akron CO, Dickinson ND, Mandan ND, Havre MT, Judith Basin MT, Sheridan WY, Archer WY, Ardmore SD, Belle Fourche SD, Garden City KS, Hays KS, Colby KS. Moisture was determined for each individual foot of soil to 6 ft. Deliverable: a digitized, bulk-density-corrected station dataset of 1906–1940 profile soil moisture for the Plains, plus the resulting skill assessment of the model ensembles currently used to characterize the 1930s.
targets.notes:
B-terms / old vocabulary for the modern quantity: 'moisture equivalent', 'wilting coefficient', 'field carrying capacity', 'minimum point of exhaustion', 'available moisture', 'percentage of water-free soil', 'moisture determinations', 'foot section' — modern terms are 'volumetric soil moisture', 'field capacity', 'wilting point', 'soil moisture anomaly', 'root-zone soil moisture'. Literatures to dig: USDA Technical Bulletin and Professional Paper series (TB 637 is the key one; Bulletin 1004; Bulletin 1139; Bulletin 402 on Akron cereal experiments 1908–1915), state agricultural experiment station Research Bulletins for NE, KS, ND, MT, CO, WY, SD (Kansas SB 273 covers Hays, Colby, Garden City moisture determinations), HathiTrust and Internet Archive for the station annual reports, USDA National Agricultural Library catalog under 'Office of Dry-Land Agriculture', and National Archives Soil Conservation Service records. Bulk density and moisture-equivalent values per station and per foot section must be harvested from the companion soil-physics bulletins, not assumed. Traps: (1) do not cite USGS WSP 820 as a soil moisture compilation — I checked, it is not; (2) do not assume the published tables are numeric (Bulletin 1139's are not); (3) RUSWET-AGROCLIM and Robock's Global Soil Moisture Data Bank cover the USSR, Illinois, China, India — NOT the pre-1950 US Plains, so do not mistake them for prior art, and do not mistake the Haas Soil Archive (Montana, soil chemistry) for soil moisture; (4) the plats are experimental treatments (fallow vs continuous cropping vs rotations), so the records are land-management-specific, not regional averages — which is actually an asset for testing the land-degradation feedback, but a confound if averaged naively; (5) station locations are agricultural research farms, not a random sample of the Plains. || PREMISES VERIFIED AT GENERATION: I fetched and extracted the full text of the primary source: Mathews, O. R., 'Storage of Water in Soil and Its Utilization by Spring Wheat', USDA Professional Paper / Bulletin 1139, 14 April 1923, with introduction by E. C. Chilcott, Agriculturist in Charge, Office of Dry-Land Agriculture Investigations, Bureau of Plant Industry. Verbatim from the extracted text, section MANNER OF STUDY: 'The moisture determinations made on the wheat plats consist of measurements of the water content of each individual foot of soil to a depth great enough to include the zone of feeding of the crop. The depth varies from 2 to 6 feet with the different soils. The moisture content is expressed as a percentage of the weight of water-free soil.' And from Chilcott's introduction: 'It has been continuous at these stations for a relatively long term of years.' Station-by-station discussion sections confirm the names listed above with per-foot results by year back to 1907. The agronomic vocabulary is confirmed verbatim in the same text: 'The minimum point of exhaustion of a soil bears a direct relation to the wilting coefficient as determined by Briggs and Shantz', and 'The moisture equivalent of each foot section of soil in the plats from which data are here presented has been determined.' I separately confirmed, via search result excerpts that I did not independently open, that Cole & Mathews, USDA Technical Bulletin 637, 'Subsoil Moisture Under Semiarid Conditions', April 1939, covers Havre, Mandan, North Platte, Hays and Colby and reports 'the yearly change in moisture content of the soil at different depths' — that is the volume that carries the record through the 1930s, and it is the first thing a scout must open; treat its contents as unverified until then. HONEST NEGATIVE: a search summary claimed a '1954 report' compiled Great Plains field soil moisture from '31 stations' with late-1930s data 'assembled but not published'. I fetched the PDF it pointed at (USGS Water-Supply Paper 820) and extracted its text: it is 'Drought of 1936', 1938, and contains no such compilation — every occurrence of 'soil moisture' in it is qualitative discussion of water-supply seasons and plant distribution. That snippet was wrong and I discarded it. Do not build on it. I also could not complete a check of whether any recent data-rescue effort has already digitized this corpus (web search budget was exhausted mid-task); confirming that is the scout's FIRST action, before any digitization. || PHYSICAL COHERENCE: Coherent and arithmetically bounded. Gravimetric percentage of oven-dry mass converts to volumetric water content as theta_v = theta_g * rho_bulk / rho_water; Plains silt loams and clay loams run rho_bulk ≈ 1.2–1.5 g/cm3, so a measured 18% by dry weight is roughly 0.22–0.27 cm3/cm3 — squarely in the range land-surface models carry, no regime problem. Six one-foot layers to 183 cm overlap the top three to four layers of typical LSM discretizations, so the comparison is layer-matched rather than extrapolated. The sampling interval is the live risk, not the physics: determinations were tied to seedbed preparation and crop growth, so the series is seasonally irregular and biased toward the growing season — it constrains growing-season depletion and interannual storage, NOT a continuous monthly climatology, and the target must be scoped to what the sampling actually supports. One more caveat found in the primary text: Bulletin 1139's published tables present per-foot results as coded categories (filled / partly wet / partly dry / etc.), not as raw percentages. The raw numeric percentages live in USDA Technical Bulletin 637, in USDA Bulletin 1004 (Cole & Mathews, 'Use of Water by Spring Wheat on the Great Plains'), in Burr, W. W., 'The storage and use of soil moisture', Nebraska Agr. Exp. Sta. Research Bulletin 5, 1914, and in the stations' annual progress reports. Confirming that numeric per-foot series actually print in TB 637 is the single pass/fail gate on this whole target. || HOW TO CHECK: Pass/fail in a single step before any heavy work: open USDA Technical Bulletin 637 (Cole & Mathews 1939, 'Subsoil Moisture Under Semiarid Conditions', ~74 pp., available at ageconsearch.umn.edu record 167381, DOI 10.22004/ag.econ.167381 — note the PDF returns HTTP 403 to plain fetchers and needs a browser or a library copy) and check whether its tables print numeric per-foot moisture percentages by year through the 1930s. If yes, the target is live: digitize, convert with per-station bulk density, and compare the resulting 1930s growing-season depletion at Hays, Colby, North Platte, Mandan and Havre against the retrospective land-surface-model soil moisture reconstructions that span 1920–2003, and against the GCM Dust Bowl attribution runs that invoke vegetation loss and dust feedbacks. A measured station series that disagrees with the ensemble in sign or magnitude at these grid cells is a publishable result; agreement is a first validation where there currently is none. If TB 637's tables turn out to be coded categories like Bulletin 1139's, fall back to Burr 1914 (Nebraska Research Bulletin 5) and the station annual reports; if those are also non-numeric, kill the target. || KILLER VERDICTS (survived 2 adversarial killers): KEEP, with mandatory downscoping. targets.problem: Glass-core package substrates and through-glass vias (TGV) are qualified with snapshot strength data (ring-on-ring / 4-point bend Weibull distributions) and pass/fail thermal-cycle counts. The glass-strength literature has, since the 1960s, treated glass strength as intrinsically TIME-dependent: subcritical (stress-corrosion) crack growth v = A*K_I^n, with measured n values and humidity dependence for soda-lime, borosilicate, fused silica and glass-ceramics, plus a worked machinery (proof-test / dynamic-fatigue / inert-strength) for converting a strength Weibull into a time-to-failure distribution under sustained load. Glass-core substrates sit under permanent sustained tensile load from redistribution-layer and Cu-plating residual stress, at room temperature, in ambient humidity - the exact regime where stress-corrosion dominates. The transfer target: take published TGV/glass-core bend-strength Weibull parameters, combine them with the existing n and B (crack-growth) parameters for the relevant alkali-free display/borosilicate glass families from the fiber-optic and architectural/structural-glass literature, and produce the first lifetime (not pass/fail) prediction for RDL-stressed glass cores - plus the proof-test screen level that would guarantee it.
targets.notes: B-terms (modern side): glass core substrate, through-glass via, TGV, panel-level packaging, RDL stress, edge crack, core cracking, Weibull fracture strength, ring-on-ring, laser-induced deep etching. B-terms (old vocabulary for the SAME physical quantity): static fatigue, delayed failure, stress corrosion of glass, subcritical crack growth, crack velocity vs stress intensity, the 'n value' / stress-corrosion susceptibility parameter, inert strength, proof testing, dynamic fatigue, universal fatigue curve, Weiderhorn region I/II/III. Literatures to dig: J. Am. Ceram. Soc. and Weiderhorn/Evans 1967-1980; the optical-fiber reliability corpus (Kurkjian, Matthewson, Glaesemann - fiber proof-test theory is the most complete engineering transfer of static fatigue to a mass-manufactured glass product); Glass Structures & Engineering and the structural-glass codes (which already contain a full lifetime-prediction formalism with n ~ 16 for soda-lime in humid air); NASA/ESA Zerodur optics-lifetime memoranda (n ~ 27-33, ln B values). Modern side: IEEE ECTC/EPTC glass-core papers 2023-2026, Micromachines 2025 FEA edge-crack papers, Corning TGV white paper, Georgia Tech PRC glass-package reliability talks. Traps: (a) the n-value apparatus is NOT dead literature - architectural glass and optical fiber use it actively, so the claim must be 'disconnected literatures', never 'nobody measured it'; (b) n is surface/flaw-population specific - a laser-ablated-plus-HF-etched TGV sidewall is not the same surface as pristine drawn glass, so the deliverable is a parameterized bound with explicit sensitivity to n, not a single number; (c) do not confuse the stress-corrosion exponent n with the Weibull modulus m, and remember a dynamic-fatigue log-log slope is 1/(n+1), not n (the patent-literature phrasing 'the stress corrosion coefficient is the slope' is a trap); (d) alkali-free glasses are expected to have higher n (less susceptible) than soda-lime - getting that direction wrong inverts the conclusion. || PREMISES VERIFIED AT GENERATION: Searched for glass-core/TGV strength and reliability data and for subcritical-crack-growth exponents. What I actually saw, as search-result extracts (I did NOT open the source pages - mdpi.com and corning.com both returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch, and api.openalex.org and api.semanticscholar.org both returned HTTP 429, so no reference list was read): a 2025 glass-substrate review record describes its scope as TGV fabrication, 'the impact of design parameters such as via density and aspect ratio on glass substrate reliability, and the mitigation strategies for stress and crack of TGV', and separately notes 'limited availability of long-term reliability data' and examination of 'the balance between redistribution-layer stress and glass fracture strength' - i.e. strength as a static quantity compared against stress, no time dependence. Corning's TGV document was reported to present 'surface strength from ring-on-ring tests plotted as Weibull distributions' and to say wafer strength and reliability 'remain to be resolved'. An Onto Innovation/LPKF piece states a small crack 'has the potential to grow into a much larger, potentially "killer" defect later'. On the old side I saw concrete n values quoted: soda-lime n=18.1 in air at 50% RH, n=16 under water, n=70 inert/vacuum; Zerodur n=30.7 with ln(B)=-6.837 at 100% humidity; 'n varying between ~12-35 for most (modified) glasses, but reaching a value of 72 for v-SiO2'. UNVERIFIED and the scout's first job: whether ANY ECTC/EPTC/Micromachines glass-core paper 2023-2026 reports a loading-rate series or an n value. Open, in order: the 2025 glass-substrate review (SUNY record), Micromachines 16(11):1256 (2025, glass-panel edge-crack FEA), and the Georgia Tech 'Reliability of Advanced Glass Packages: Past, Present and Future' talk. If any of them fits a crack-velocity law to TGV coupons, this target is dead - say so immediately. || PHYSICAL COHERENCE: Coherent and in the right regime. Subcritical crack growth in silicate glass is a room-temperature, ambient-humidity, sustained-load phenomenon - precisely the service condition of a glass core carrying frozen-in RDL and Cu-plating stress for years, and precisely why it is invisible to short thermal-cycle tests. Driving stresses are in the right band: reported glass-core edge stresses of order 50-95 MPa and RDL-induced core stresses of tens of MPa sit well below the instantaneous bend strength (hundreds of MPa) but comfortably inside region-I crack growth, which is exactly the condition under which static fatigue, not fast fracture, sets lifetime. Arithmetic check on the payoff: with a power law of exponent n, time-to-failure scales as stress^-n, so for n=18 a factor-2 stress reduction (the reported 95 -> 49 MPa edge-stress improvement) buys ~2^18 ~ 2.6e5 in lifetime, while for n=30 it buys ~1e9 - the ORDER of the answer depends entirely on an n the packaging literature has not measured. That sensitivity is the target's value, and it is also the honest statement of its uncertainty. No pressure/temperature incoherence: everything happens at 1 atm and 20-85 C. || HOW TO CHECK: High and cheap. Step 1 (kill-or-keep, hours): read the reference lists and methods of the three modern documents named above and grep for n-value / loading-rate / crack-velocity / proof-test. Step 2: extract published TGV and glass-core strength Weibull parameters (scale and modulus, with the test geometry and effective area) from ECTC/EPTC and vendor papers. Step 3: extract n and B for the matching glass chemistries (alkali-free aluminoborosilicate, borosilicate, fused silica) from the fiber-optic and structural-glass corpora, with humidity stated. Step 4: compute time-to-failure distributions and the proof-test stress needed for a 10-year, ppm-level failure target, reported as a band over n = 15-35. Falsifiable output: a numeric lifetime bound and a proof-screen level, either of which a bend-test-plus-loading-rate experiment on real TGV coupons can confirm or refute.

targets.problem: Soft-robotics and microfluidic "fluidic logic" groups (2018-2026) build pneumatic circuits out of snap-through bistable membrane valves and repeatedly hit the same three walls: low pressure gain per element, inability to cascade more than a few stages without an added "power amplifier", and DC bias / flow-noise accumulation between stages. The quantitative design answers to all three were published 1965-1990 for jet-deflection Laminar Proportional Amplifiers (LPAs) and laminar fluidic logic, in the SAME Reynolds-number regime, and that corpus is absent from the modern reference lists. Task for the scout: extract the dimensionless design rules (aspect ratio, setback, control length, receiver distance and width, center-vent width, bias pressure), the measured gain-per-stage envelope, the impedance-matching / staging rules, and the noise-and-bias mitigation methods, and state them in modern soft-robotics units (kPa, mm, SLPM).
targets.notes: B-terms / OLD vocabulary for the same physics: 'fluid amplifier', 'fluerics', 'fluidics', 'laminar proportional amplifier (LPA)', 'beam-deflection amplifier', 'wall-attachment element', 'bistable flip-flop', 'gainblock', 'staging', 'impedance matching', 'vent pressure referencing', 'setback', 'receiver distance', 'aspect ratio' (nozzle depth/width). MODERN vocabulary: 'soft fluidic logic', 'soft bistable valve', 'pneumatic transistor', 'microfluidic logic', 'electronics-free control', 'fan-out', 'cascadability'. Where to dig: DTIC (Harry Diamond Laboratories / HDL-TR, Adelphi MD - try report numbers near ADA030673), NASA NTRS (Hellbaum, LaRC), ASME Journal of Fluids Engineering 1966-1985, the ASME/HDL fluidics symposium volumes, US patents 3986527, 4441526, 4934409 (their prior-art lists are a free bibliography of the dead field), the Proceedings of the Cranfield Fluidics Conferences, and Kirshner & Katz 'Design Theory of Fluidic Components'. TRAPS: (1) do not claim nobody has measured soft-gate gain - they have; the claim is that the DESIGN RULES already exist. (2) Much of the corpus is oil/water or high-pressure air hydraulics - filter by nozzle Reynolds number, not by working fluid. (3) Several HDL devices were turbulent-reattachment (Re 1e4+) devices; those are the WRONG scope condition for mm-scale soft robots and will not transfer - only the explicitly laminar subset does. (4) 'Fluidic oscillator' hits will be dominated by the aerospace flow-control revival; exclude those to find the logic literature. || PREMISES VERIFIED AT GENERATION: (1) NTRS 19760014347, R. F. Hellbaum, NASA Langley, 1976, 'Experimental design of laminar proportional amplifiers' - I read the record and it states the program varied 'aspect ratio, setback, control length, receiver distance and width, center vent width, and bias pressure' and covered 'matching and staging amplifiers for high pressure gain', with the explicit results 'Usable pressure gains from 4 to 19 per stage can now be achieved' and 'five amplifiers were staged together to yield pressure gains up to 2,000,000'. (2) I downloaded the full PDF of Kendre, Whiteside, Fan, Tracz, Teran, Underwood, Sayed, Jiang, Stokes, Preston, Whitesides & Nemitz, 'The Soft Compiler: A Web-Based Tool for the Design of Modular Pneumatic Circuits for Soft Robots', IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters 7(3):6060-6066 (2022), ran pdftotext on it, and inspected the bibliography and every 4-digit year in the file. The oldest substantive reference is 2004 (Blaya & Herr); the only pre-1990 digit strings in the file are artifacts inside a DOI ('10.1002/adma.201701985') and a mangled DOI string ('10.1109/tce.1953.637193'). There is no citation to Hellbaum, Kirshner, Drzewiecki, Harry Diamond Laboratories, laminar proportional amplifiers, or any 1960s-80s fluidics source. Its own framing of the problem is cascading and wiring complexity ('a soft circuit with 10 soft valves requires up to 60 tubes'), and it points to Rothemund's soft bistable valve and Preston's gates as the primitives. (3) A US Army patent (US 4,934,409, 'T junction interconnected multistage fluidic gainblock') is explicitly about 'reduction of flow noise and DC bias between stages of Laminar Proportional Amplifiers' - i.e. the exact failure mode modern soft circuits report. I did NOT verify a Drzewiecki authorship attribution; search snippets would not confirm it, so the scout should treat that name as unconfirmed and work from Hellbaum plus the HDL report series. || PHYSICAL COHERENCE: Regimes overlap, so the transfer is numerically possible. Soft pneumatic logic: air, channel/orifice ~0.5-2 mm, supply 10-100 kPa, flows of order 0.1-1 standard L/min. Arithmetic: 1 SLPM = 1.67e-5 m^3/s; through a 1 mm x 1 mm nozzle that is ~16.7 m/s; Re = rho*V*D/mu = 1.2 * 16.7 * 1e-3 / 1.8e-5 ~ 1.1e3. Published LPA operation sits at nozzle Reynolds numbers of roughly 5e2-2.5e3 with nozzle widths of a few tenths of a mm to ~1 mm and supply pressures of order 1-10 kPa. Same fluid, same Re decade, same length scale, compressibility negligible (Mach << 0.1 at these velocities). The one genuine incoherence to flag: LPA gains are quoted as PRESSURE gain into a matched high-impedance load, whereas soft valves are usually characterized by threshold/hysteresis pressures and flow capacity into an actuator with large compliance, so a scout must re-express LPA staging rules in terms of load impedance before claiming a number transfers. Bias/vent referencing is the part that transfers most cleanly and is also the cheapest to test. || HOW TO CHECK: Bounded and cheap. (a) Pull Hellbaum 1976 (NTRS 19760014347) and 3-5 HDL fluerics reports from DTIC free-text search, and tabulate the dimensionless geometry sweeps and gain-per-stage data. (b) Citation test: take the 6-10 most-cited post-2017 soft/microfluidic logic papers (Rothemund 2018 soft bistable valve; Preston PNAS 2019 digital logic; Preston oscillator paper; Nemitz non-volatile fluidic memory; Wehner/Octobot Nature 2016; the Kendre 2022 Soft Compiler; any 2024-2026 review) and count citations to any pre-1995 fluidics source. Prediction: zero or near-zero. One hit does not kill the target; a modern review with a 1960s-fluidics section does. (c) Physical test, one afternoon on a benchtop: fabricate a single-stage planar LPA at the published optimum geometry in PDMS or by laser-cutting acrylic, drive it at 2-20 kPa air, and measure differential output pressure vs differential control pressure to see whether gain lands in the published 4-19 band at mm scale. (d) Bias/vent test: on an existing 3-5 gate soft circuit, add the published symmetric-vent referencing and T-junction interstage coupling and measure whether the stage-to-stage DC bias drift that currently forces re-tuning is reduced. Each of these fails fast and publicly.
targets.domain: Fluid mechanics, rheology, multiphase flow and mixing

targets.problem: Scale-up of solid-state fermentation is still described as unsolved: the standard reference work (Mitchell, Krieger and Berovic, Solid-State Fermentation Bioreactors, Springer 2006) states that there are many SSF bioreactors, especially in the koji industry, but little or no information about the efficiency of heat and mass transfer within them, and a 2019 tray-bioreactor paper still reports no reliable scaling methodology and bed gradients up to 10 degC. Meanwhile the Japanese sake, miso and shoyu industries industrialised exactly this - forced-aeration automatic koji-making machines from about 1960, in internal-aeration, surface-aeration, rotating-drum and non-aerated configurations, at 1-30 tonne bed scale - and the design and operating data for them were published in Japanese-language society journals, industry association reports and patents. Target: recover measured bed temperature profiles, aeration rates per unit bed mass, water-balance and evaporative-cooling data, and the documented failure mode (aeration holds product temperature but under-evaporates surface moisture) from the Japanese corpus, and convert them into the heat- and mass-transfer coefficients the English SSF modelling literature says it lacks.
targets.notes: B-terms and the OLD/other vocabulary for the same physical quantities - this is the whole target, so get them right: 製麹 (seikiku, koji making), 自動製麹装置 (automatic koji-making machine), 通風製麹 (forced-aeration koji making), 通風式固体培養装置 (aerated solid-culture apparatus), 麹層 (koji bed), 品温 (product temperature - note: heat removal is written as a product-temperature CONTROL problem, never as a heat-transfer coefficient, which is the vocabulary split), 手入れ (mixing/turning), 回転ドラム式 (rotating drum), 無通風 (non-aerated). Where to comb: J-STAGE for 日本醸造協会誌 / 日本醸造協会雑誌 and 発酵工学雑誌 (Journal of Fermentation Technology) back issues, which are largely free; Google Patents in Japanese (e.g. JP3046321B2 on control of aerated solid-culture apparatus, JPH05292939A on automatic product-temperature control in koji apparatus) - patents state setpoints, airflow and control laws; JSPMI (jspmi.or.jp) machine-industry award write-ups and equipment-maker technical histories (Fujiwara Techno-Art) for the documented engineering failure modes. TRAPS: (1) Do NOT write the premise as 'the English literature ignores Japanese koji work' - it does cite the English-published Japanese papers (rotating-drum and aerated-bed studies in Hakkokogaku Zasshi/J. Ferment. Technol.), so a loose brief gets falsified in one search; the claim is strictly about the Japanese-only subset. (2) Nagel's 2002 thesis and the Mitchell group already model wall-cooling insufficiency above about 2 m3 for A. oryzae, so do not present the heat-removal limit itself as unknown - what is missing is measured tonne-scale parameters, not awareness of the problem. (3) Machine-vendor histories are promotional; treat them as pointers to the failure modes, then find the data. || PREMISES VERIFIED AT GENERATION: WebSearch, 2026-10-20, including a Japanese-language query. Search-result summaries reported: the Mitchell/Krieger/Berovic Springer volume stating there were many SSF bioreactors, especially those used in the koji industry, but little or no information about the efficiency of heat and mass transfer processes within them; a 2019 AIDIC/ECCE tray-bioreactor paper stating there is still no reliable methodology to scale the process and citing gradients up to 10 degC; Nagel's 2002 thesis finding wall cooling insufficient at about 2 m3 scale for a rapidly growing fungus like A. oryzae. Japanese-side: a koji-machine explanatory page (nada-ken.com) describing manual koji making being simplified and automated from about 1960 with several machine types commercialised, the operating principle being to pass temperature- and humidity-conditioned air through the koji bed to remove its metabolic heat, and classifying aeration as internal, surface, rotating-drum and non-aerated; a JSPMI PDF (jspmi.or.jp N01-08) stating that aeration succeeded in holding product temperature correctly but that moisture evaporation from the koji surface was inadequate, motivating a non-aerated automatic method; Japanese patents JP3046321B2 and JPH05292939A on aerated-solid-culture temperature control. I did NOT locate a specific 1960s 日本醸造協会誌 engineering paper or open the Mitchell book's bibliography - both are required first steps and either could kill this target. || PHYSICAL COHERENCE: Coherent; all at ambient pressure and mesophilic temperature. The regime is a packed bed of steamed rice or soy at roughly 30-40 degC with A. oryzae, cooled almost entirely by evaporation plus sensible heat in the air stream. The order of magnitude is right: fungal SSF metabolic heat is of order 100-400 kJ per kg dry substrate per hour at peak, and latent heat of vaporisation near 2440 kJ/kg, so peak cooling needs roughly 0.04-0.16 kg water evaporated per kg dry substrate per hour - which is exactly why the Japanese reports describe the binding constraint as surface moisture loss and product drying rather than as a temperature-control failure, and why conduction through walls fails above a few m3. The two corpora are describing the same physics in the same regime with no extrapolation needed; the bridge requires the same sign of the effect (more aeration removes more heat AND more water) in both, which is the documented behaviour on both sides. || HOW TO CHECK: Moderate to high, with a language cost. Decisive cheap checks: (1) open the Mitchell 2006 bibliography and the reference lists of two recent SSF scale-up reviews and count Japanese-language entries - near-zero Japanese-only entries alongside present English-published Japanese entries confirms the premise as stated; (2) search J-STAGE in Japanese for 製麹 / 通風 / 麹層 温度 restricted to 1960-1990 and confirm that at least one paper reports a measured bed temperature profile or water balance at pilot or production scale. Falsifiable in a few hours by a scout who can read Japanese; if no tonne-scale measurements exist and the Japanese corpus is purely descriptive or purely apparatus patents, kill it - patents alone (setpoints without measured profiles) are not enough to support the claim.
