targets.problem: Polaroid and Kodak built self-contained, temperature-aware chemical clocks into instant-film sheets: a polymeric acid layer separated from the image layers by a 'timing layer' whose alkali permeability was deliberately tuned so that the pH crash terminating development arrived at the right moment at both 5 °C and 40 °C. In doing so they measured, across many polymer chemistries, the ACTIVATION ENERGY OF PENETRATION BY AQUEOUS ALKALI — including a set of polymers with INVERSE temperature dependence (hydroxypropyl cellulose, polyvinyl methyl ether, polyethylene oxide, polyvinyl oxazolidinone, hydroxypropyl methylcellulose) — plus 'barrier' timing layers that start impermeable and switch on after hydrolysis or neutralisation. Paper-microfluidic and lateral-flow diagnostics now need exactly this: passive timers that gate sequential reagent delivery in an instrument-free device used anywhere from a cold clinic to a hot field site. That community builds sugar bridges, pullulan films, wax prints, laser-written hydrophobic barriers and flow shunts, has no Ea-vs-chemistry library at all, and lists ambient temperature as future work. Task: port the Polaroid/Kodak Ea library and the barrier-timing-layer architecture into paper and membrane timers.
targets.notes: B-TERMS (the bridging concepts): activation energy of aqueous-reagent penetration through a thin polymer barrier; the latency-then-switch architecture of a barrier layer that is initially impermeable and is turned on by its own hydrolysis or neutralisation; deliberate matching of a barrier's temperature coefficient to the temperature coefficient of the reaction it gates. OLD VOCABULARY to search with: timing layer, barrier timing layer, polymeric acid layer, spacer layer, alkali permeability, activation energy of penetration, inverse temperature-dependent permeability, latex timing layer, temperature-responsive timing, premature pH drop. NEW VOCABULARY on the other side: fluidic time delay, delay valve, dissolvable bridge, erodible polymeric bridge, shunt, sequential reagent delivery, programmable paper device, instrument-free multi-step assay. WHERE TO DIG: USPTO/Espacenet assignee=Polaroid, 1965–1996, and assignee=Eastman Kodak 1976–1986 (the PR-10 instant line) in G03C 8/; Photographic Science and Engineering 1968–1984; the Fuji instant-film patent family for a third independent dataset. TRAPS: (1) THE SIGN TRAP IS THE WHOLE RISK HERE — see core_premise. Never write that Polaroid achieved temperature-independent timing; they deliberately achieved temperature-TRACKING timing. The deliverable is the Ea library and both of its signs. (2) Do not claim instant film died — it was restarted by Impossible Project / Polaroid Originals from the Enschede plant; the correct claim is that the quantitative design corpus was not transferred, and the modern film's temperature sensitivity is the evidence. (3) Do not attribute the patent quotes to Land or Rogers; no source I saw named an inventor, and misquoting the source is failure pattern 3. (4) Thermally actuated wax-ink valves already exist in paper microfluidics (a patent on resistor-heated wax valves came up in my search) — those are ACTIVE heating, a different thing from a passive barrier with engineered Ea; keep the distinction or a reviewer will call the gap closed. (5) Nitrocellulose and paper are porous media, not cast polymer films; breakthrough through a porous membrane couples capillarity to permeation, so the old Ea values are a design library to be re-measured in the new material class, not numbers to be transplanted. || CORE PREMISE + SELF-ATTACK: The instant-photography corpus contains measured activation energies for aqueous-alkali (and more generally aqueous-reagent) penetration of specific coatable polymers, spanning both signs of temperature dependence, and no paper-microfluidic or lateral-flow time-delay paper uses, cites, or reproduces that library — although both are solving the identical problem of setting a reagent-arrival time in a passive, instrument-free layered device. SELF-ATTACK, and the thing most likely to kill a sloppy version of this: THE TWO FIELDS WANT OPPOSITE THINGS. Polaroid wanted the timer to TRACK development, so it deliberately chose HIGH Ea (>18 kcal/mol) to make the barrier more permeable when warm. A diagnostic timer usually wants the delay to be temperature-INVARIANT, which needs LOW Ea. If a scout writes 'Polaroid solved temperature-compensated timing, so reuse their polymer,' that is failure pattern 6 and the target dies. The transferable asset is NOT a solution but the MEASUREMENT SET: a sign-and-magnitude library of Ea across polymer chemistries, from which a modern designer can pick near-zero-Ea for invariance, positive Ea to track a temperature-sensitive enzyme step, or an inverse-Ea polymer to over-compensate. Any proposal built on 'they already solved it' must be rejected. || DISCONTINUITY: Two dated severances, not one. (1) 9 January 1986: Eastman Kodak was forced out of instant photography by the injunction in Polaroid's patent suit, which terminated its entire parallel body of instant-film timing and pH-barrier chemistry. (I have NOT verified this date by search in this session — it is from prior knowledge and a scout must confirm it before quoting.) (2) February 2008 (reported 8–10 February; sources differ on the day): Polaroid announced it would stop making instant film and close its plants in Massachusetts, Mexico and the Netherlands; the Enschede plant closed in June 2008, with its remaining ~160 staff — down from a peak of ~1,200 — made redundant. CRITICAL NUANCE that a scout must handle honestly rather than hide: instant film did NOT stay dead. Former Enschede employees founded Impossible Project / Polaroid Originals and restarted production. But they restarted WITHOUT the reagent and timing-layer know-how, had to reinvent the chemistry, and the modern film's well-known temperature sensitivity and long, fussy development is the direct observable evidence that the timing-layer design knowledge was lost rather than inherited. The discontinuity is the loss of the quantitative design corpus, which is exactly why it is still recoverable from patents and not from anyone's bench. || PREMISES VERIFIED: (a) WebSearch on 'Polaroid SX-70 "timing layer" polymeric acid alkali permeability temperature compensation' returned ten hits, all patents, eight assigned to Polaroid. Claim text I actually saw, quoted: US 4,056,394 — 'It has now been found that a timing layer which is more alkali-permeable at higher temperatures and less permeable at lower temperatures can be produced by employing a polymeric latex having an activation energy of penetration by an aqueous alkaline solution of greater than 18 kcal/mole'; and 'Typically, timing layers have been designed so as to offer temperature responses substantially parallel to that of the development process.' A second Polaroid patent lists polymers with INVERSE temperature-dependent alkali permeability: 'hydroxypropyl cellulose; polyvinyl methyl ether; polyethylene oxide; polyvinyl oxazolidinone; hydroxypropyl methyl cellulose.' A third describes barrier timing layers: 'A barrier timing layer is initially substantially impermeable and time is required to allow the aqueous alkaline solution to react with the layer and increase its permeability. Usually the permeability increasing reaction that takes place is the hydrolysis or neutralization of the layer by the alkaline solution.' Candidate nodes seen: US 4,056,394; 4,359,517; 5,593,810; 5,604,079; 4,304,850; 4,407,938. NOTE: these are search-returned claim excerpts; I have not read any patent in full and I attribute none of this to Land or Rogers, because no source I saw named them. (b) I opened the most on-point modern document and read it: 'Tunable-Delay Shunts for Paper Microfluidic Devices', https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3950207/ . It has 24 references, covering paper diagnostics, wax/surfactant/magnetic valves and Washburn flow. NOT ONE reference concerns photographic diffusion transfer, Polaroid, instant film, timing layers or alkali-permeable barrier layers. It reports delays of 3 to ~20 min with CVs of 3.8–8.0% (shunt length) and 1.4–5.9% (thickness), controlled humidity at 75% RH, and does NOT control or report temperature — it defers it, in the paper's own words, to 'quantification of the effects of varying environmental conditions, i.e. humidity levels and temperature'. That is the gap, stated by the receiving field itself. (c) A separate search of the modern delay-valve literature surfaced sugar/pullulan dissolvable valves, wax-printed delays, laser-written hydrophobic barriers and thermally actuated wax-ink valves, and returned NO source quantifying how ambient temperature shifts a passive barrier delay. (d) Polaroid 2008 closure details confirmed from secondary reporting only; the Enschede June 2008 date and the ~160/1,200 headcount came from press and interview accounts, not a company filing. || COHERENCE: Arithmetic checked, and it is the load-bearing part of this target. Ea = 18 kcal/mol = 75.3 kJ/mol. Over the stated 5–40 °C working range: ratio = exp[(75300/8.314)(1/278.15 − 1/313.15)] = exp[9057 × (3.5951e-3 − 3.1934e-3)] = exp[9057 × 4.017e-4] = exp(3.64) ≈ 38. So a >18 kcal/mol barrier changes its permeability roughly 38-fold across 5–40 °C — the right order to offset a silver-halide development rate whose own Ea is in the same 15–20 kcal/mol band, which makes Polaroid's stated design intent numerically sensible rather than marketing. For a diagnostic timer the same arithmetic sets the budget the other way: to hold a 10-minute delay within ±10% from 15 °C to 35 °C you need an effective Ea below about 2 kcal/mol, i.e. a near-athermal barrier, which is precisely the regime no modern sugar- or wax-based valve can be in (sucrose/pullulan dissolution and wax softening are both strongly thermally activated, and wax has a melting transition inside the ambient range). That is the quantitative statement of the opportunity. Regime: everything is aqueous, atmospheric pressure, 5–40 °C, millimetre-scale layers — no pressure or temperature regime jump anywhere in the bridge. Sign: explicitly handled above and in core_premise; both signs exist in the old library, so the bridge does not require inverting an effect, it requires choosing from a measured set. || HOW TO CHECK: Falsifiable in three steps, cheapest first. STEP 1 (kills it): full-text search Lab on a Chip, Analytical Chemistry, Biosensors & Bioelectronics, ACS Sensors and Microfluidics & Nanofluidics, 2010–2026, for 'timing layer', 'diffusion transfer', 'Polaroid', 'polymeric acid layer', and for 'activation energy' co-occurring with 'time delay' or 'delay valve'. Any paper-fluidic timer paper that reports an Arrhenius Ea for its barrier, or cites the instant-film corpus, kills the target. STEP 2 (kills it the other way): pull US 4,056,394, US 4,359,517 and US 5,593,810 in full from Google Patents and confirm the patents contain actual MEASURED Ea values or breakthrough-time-vs-temperature data for NAMED polymers — not merely the claim language of a threshold. If the >18 kcal/mol figure is only a claim limit with no supporting table, the library does not exist and the target is padding. STEP 3 only if both pass: cast the two or three named inverse-temperature polymers (HPC, HPMC, PEO) and two or three high-Ea latices as thin barriers on nitrocellulose, measure breakthrough time at 15, 25 and 35 °C, fit Ea, and test whether any composition reaches the <2 kcal/mol athermal target computed above. Pass/fail is a single number per material.
targets.domain: Photography, film, printing and imaging chemistry before digital

targets.problem: Groundwater models worldwide (MODFLOW EVT, ETS1, and the RIP-ET package) require the evapotranspiration rate of phreatophytic vegetation as a FUNCTION of depth to the water table — operationally an 'extinction depth' plus, in RIP-ET, a segmented dimensionless ET-vs-depth curve per plant functional group. Modern practice supplies these numbers from rooting-depth proxies, soil-physics model inversions (Shah/Nachabe/Ross-type), remote-sensing ET regressions, or calibration. But between roughly 1958 and 1974 the USGS ran large outdoor evapotranspirometer tanks — undisturbed or reconstructed soil columns, ~1,000 ft2 each, planted with single phreatophyte species, with the water table HELD at several fixed depths for multiple growing seasons — and published the resulting water use directly. That is a direct, controlled measurement of exactly the constitutive function the models guess at. Task: extract the per-species ET-vs-water-table-depth response curves (and the implied extinction depths) from USGS Professional Papers 491-E (Van Hylckama 1974, saltcedar, water-budget method), 486-F (McDonald & Hughes 1968, Yuma tanks 1961-66: arrowweed, saltbush, quailbrush, bermudagrass), Water-Supply Paper 1423 (Robinson 1958), and the Professional Paper 655 series (Gila River Phreatophyte Project), convert them to the dimensionless RIP-ET curve form, and compare against the curve shapes and extinction depths actually in use.
targets.notes: B-terms / bridging quantity: ET as a function of depth to water table. OLD vocabulary: 'water use by phreatophytes', 'water salvage', 'evapotranspirometer tank', 'tank water use', 'depth to water', 'bottom-land vegetation', 'consumptive use in acre-feet per acre', 'reclaimable water'. NEW vocabulary: 'groundwater evapotranspiration', 'extinction depth', 'saturated extinction depth', 'groundwater-dependent ecosystem water requirement', 'ET flux rate curve', 'plant functional group'. Where to dig: USGS Professional Paper series 486 (parts A-F), 491 (parts A-E), 655 (parts A-P); USGS Water-Supply Papers 1103 (Gatewood et al. 1950, Safford Valley) and 1423 (Robinson 1958); Western Snow/AGU-era state engineer reports; Bureau of Reclamation phreatophyte-control reports; Texas Water Development Board numbered reports (e.g. R168). TRAPS: (1) Do NOT claim the old corpus is uncited — Gatewood 1950 and Van Hylckama 1974 ARE cited by the modern riparian-ET community (Glenn, Nagler, and the Pecos/Colorado saltcedar salvage papers cite them routinely). The premise is specifically about the DEPTH-RESPONSE FUNCTION being unextracted, not about citation. (2) Van Hylckama's Buckeye tanks used saline groundwater and included periodic flushing; salinity co-varies with depth treatment in parts of that record — the scout must separate the salinity effect from the depth effect or the curve is confounded. (3) McDonald & Hughes 1968 did NOT include saltcedar; do not merge species across reports carelessly. (4) Tank sidewalls suppress advection and alter the energy balance relative to a wide stand — the extracted curve is a SHAPE constraint, not an absolute flux. (5) First read the 'development of the ET curves' section of Maddock, Baird, Hanson, Schmid & Ajami (2012), USGS Techniques and Methods 6-A39, before asserting the curves came from elsewhere; I did not get that section open. || CORE PREMISE: The ET-vs-depth-to-water-table response functions measured directly in the 1958-1974 USGS phreatophyte tank experiments have NOT been extracted and used to parameterize the ET-vs-depth curves (extinction depth, saturated extinction depth, segment geometry) in current groundwater-ET packages; those parameters are instead derived from rooting-depth proxies, soil-physics inversions, or calibration. || DISCONTINUITY: Federal phreatophyte-eradication-for-water-salvage was abandoned as a policy objective in the 1970s, and the USGS research programme built to quantify it was wound down with it. The concrete anchor: the Gila River Phreatophyte Project (Graham County, Arizona), whose objectives-and-methods volume is USGS Professional Paper 655-A (published 1970) and whose terminal volume is Professional Paper 655-P, 'Evapotranspiration Before and After Clearing Phreatophytes, Gila River Flood Plain, Graham County, Arizona' (Culler and others, 1982) — described by USGS as the LAST of the Professional Paper 655 series. The companion tank programme ended in the same window: McDonald & Hughes's Yuma tanks ran 1961-66 (PP 486-F, 1968) and Van Hylckama's saltcedar tank record terminated with PP 491-E (1974). No comparable controlled-water-table-depth tank programme has been run in the United States since. The policy severance is bracketed by NEPA (1970) and the Endangered Species Act (1973), after which riparian vegetation ceased to be a federally fundable eradication target. || GAP MECHANISM: Not bibliographic — the question itself was re-posed with the opposite sign of intent, and the physical quantity was renamed. The old programme existed to answer 'how much water can be SALVAGED by removing this vegetation', so its deliverable was consumptive use in acre-feet per acre at a managed water-table depth, published in USGS Professional Papers as a water-supply accounting figure. After eradication became legally and politically dead, the same physical quantity was re-asked as 'how much water does this groundwater-dependent ECOSYSTEM require', and its deliverable became a model input parameter named 'extinction depth' in groundwater-flow code documentation. Same physical function, opposite policy intent, different units (acre-feet/acre/yr vs. m/d flux and a dimensionless curve), and different publication venue (1950s-70s Professional Papers vs. post-2000 USGS Techniques and Methods software documentation and ecohydrology journals). The modern groundwater-modelling community that needs the parameter does not share a reading list with the riparian-ET ecology community that does cite the old papers — so the old papers are cited for their FLUX TOTALS by ecologists and never mined for their DEPTH DERIVATIVE by modellers. || PREMISES VERIFIED: VERIFIED DIRECTLY (I opened the page): https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/pp491E returns 'Water use by saltcedar as measured by the water budget method', T. E. Van Hylckama, 1974, USGS Professional Paper 491-E, 29 p. The page carries no abstract and does NOT list tank count, tank size, or the water-table depths — those must be read from the PDF (https://pubs.usgs.gov/pp/0491e/report.pdf, which exceeded my fetch size limit; the scout should page it). VERIFIED FROM SEARCH-RESULT TEXT, NOT READ IN FULL (flagging this honestly, not as 'verified live'): (a) PP 491-E's figure list includes a 1965 bar graph of tank water use showing 'the effect of depth to water and flushing of saline groundwater' — this is the single most load-bearing unverified item and the scout must confirm it first; (b) McDonald & Hughes 1968, PP 486-F, ran controlled tank experiments near Yuma, Arizona 1961-66 with tanks of about 1,000 square feet for most species, covering arrowweed, saltbush, quailbrush and bermudagrass; (c) USGS describes PP 655-P (Culler and others, 1982) as the last of the Professional Paper 655 series on the Gila River Phreatophyte Project, with PP 655-A dated 1970 and 655-D dated 1971. MODERN SIDE VERIFIED FROM USGS DOCUMENTATION PAGES: the RIP-ET package (Maddock, Baird, Hanson, Schmid & Ajami 2012, USGS TM 6-A39) 'replaces this traditional relationship with a segmented, nonlinear dimensionless curve that reflects the eco-physiology of riparian and wetland ecosystems'; ModelMuse's Riparian ET Plant Groups dialog exposes 'Dimensionless active root depth segment (fdh)', 'Dimensionless flux segment (fdR)', and 'Evaporative flux at saturated extinction depth (Rsxd)'; the standard EVT package requires only 'ET surface, maximum ET rate, and extinction depth'. NOT VERIFIED, AND THE DECISIVE CHECK THE SCOUT MUST RUN FIRST: the provenance of the RIP-ET curve shapes. I could not open the curve-development section of TM 6-A39, and my search returned no statement of its data source. If that section cites the 1958-74 tank experiments, the core premise is FALSE and the target dies immediately. Also unverified: whether Shah, Nachabe & Ross (2007) extinction depths were derived from these tanks (I believe they were model-derived, but did not confirm). OPENALEX WAS UNAVAILABLE (free daily budget for this IP exhausted, HTTP 429), so the bare-concept co-occurrence check on 'evapotranspirometer tank' x 'extinction depth' was NOT run — the scout must run it before anything else. || HOW TO CHECK: Highly verifiable and cheap. All primary sources are free USGS PDFs at stable URLs (pubs.usgs.gov/pp/0491e/, /pp/0486f/, /pp/0655p/, /pp/0655a/, /wsp/1423/). The old reports tabulate tank water use by treatment and year, so the depth-response curve can be digitized from printed tables rather than inferred. The modern side is equally open: USGS TM 6-A39 and the MODFLOW/ModelMuse documentation state the required parameters explicitly, and published model reports for Arizona/New Mexico/Nevada basins list the extinction depths actually used, so the comparison is a direct numerical one. KILL CONDITION, to be checked in the first 20 minutes: open the ET-curve-development section of TM 6-A39 and the reference lists of two post-2010 basin models using RIP-ET. If either cites PP 486-F, 491-E, or the PP 655 series as the source of the curve shape or extinction depth, report the target dead and stop.
targets.domain: Measurement series that ran for decades and then stopped: tide gauges, evaporation pans, snow courses, river gauging, soil surveys, phenology networks

targets.problem: Modern two-dimensional firn rheology (the Gagliardini–Meyssonnier compressible-viscous law, as recalibrated by Arrizabalaga-Iriarte et al. 2025) is unconstrained in low-density near-surface firn because its compressibility parameter k can only be fitted against deviatoric/non-hydrostatic loading, and the authors could locate exactly ONE such validation experiment: the 3-year collapse of a single balloon-cast tunnel at NEEM, which they themselves discount because of the anomalous warm summers of 2012–2014. The US Army's 1955–1966 undersnow-construction programme instrumented dozens of trench and tunnel cross-sections at Camp Century, Camp Fistclench, Site 2, Byrd Station and Tuto and tracked their closure for up to seven years at known depth, density, temperature and span. The task: recover those closure/deformation records and the companion plate-load and spread-foundation creep tests, convert them from engineering units (inches or feet per year of span loss, psi bearing stress) into strain-rate/effective-stress pairs, and use them as the multi-geometry, multi-site, cold-site calibration set for k and for the primary-creep stage that the modern literature says it cannot validate.
targets.notes: B-terms / old vocabulary: 'closure of undersnow openings', 'trench closure rate', 'snow creep', 'natural consolidation of snow', 'movement record', 'cross-section measurement station', 'Helipot settlement recorder', 'useful life of undersnow facilities', 'snow bearing capacity', 'plate-load test on processed snow'. Modern vocabulary for the same physical quantity: 'firn densification', 'firn compaction', 'compressibility parameter k', 'relative density', 'bubble close-off'. Dig in: DTIC (AD0430148 = CRREL TR 121, Waterhouse, Tobiasson & Scott, 'Camp Century movement record', May 1963 — 18 cross-section stations plus 29 movement-recording Helipots, first readings Aug 1959); ERDC-Library jspui (CRREL Technical Reports, Special Reports SR-44, SR-56 Leighty 1963, SR-90, SR-150 Kovacs 1970 'Camp Century revisited'); AD0407076 'Byrd Station snow tunnels — wall clearing study' (reports closure rates in most tunnels); Clark 1965 CRREL TR 174; Edgar's CRREL paper on sublimation for snow removal (gives ~1 ft/yr combined plastic-flow + densification closure). TRAPS: (1) Camp Century trenches carried heated glycol lines and a reactor/steam plant — Kovacs 1970 explicitly attributes accelerated local closure to that heat, so segregate heated from unheated reaches or the inversion will return a spuriously soft rheology; (2) much of the camp was built in Peter-plow-processed, artificially sintered snow whose density history differs from natural firn — use the measured density profile, never a site average; (3) do not reuse trench reaches that had been mechanically re-trimmed ('wall clearing'), since the span was reset; (4) the engineering reports give span loss, not strain rate — you must divide by original span and reconstruct the overburden stress from the measured density profile, not from an assumed 917 kg/m3. || CORE PREMISE: The 2-D firn-densification literature that needs non-hydrostatic low-density-firn validation data does not cite the 1959–1966 CRREL instrumented undersnow-closure datasets, even though those datasets measure exactly the quantity it lacks (cavity closure rate in firn of 0.40–0.60 Mg/m3 under 0.02–0.08 MPa at -20 to -29 C), and they are substantial enough to constrain k. || DISCONTINUITY: Camp Century was deactivated and Project Iceworm cancelled in 1966 (the PM-2A reactor had already been removed in 1964); with that the US Army Polar Research and Development Center's deep-snow undersnow-construction mission ended, and CRREL's programme of instrumented cavity-closure measurement in polar firn stopped. No comparable instrumented undersnow-cavity programme has existed since. The 1959–1966 output therefore sits in Army technical-report grey literature (DTIC/ERDC-Library), issued before the glaciological firn-densification literature (Herron & Langway 1980 onward) existed as a field. || GAP MECHANISM: Not a citation-count gap but a scope-condition-and-units split. The old corpus exists to answer 'how many years until this trench must be abandoned', and reports span loss in inches per year against bearing stress in psi for a man-made, often artificially sintered and locally heated cavity. The modern corpus exists to convert satellite elevation change into mass change, and reports density against depth in kg/m3 for undisturbed natural firn under self-weight. The two never share a search term for the same tensor quantity. Compounding it, the data live in Army grey literature that the glaciology community does not index, while the cold-regions engineering community that DOES know them (ERDC's own snow-foundation creep report validates its secondary-creep model against the Camp Century spread-foundation settlement and states it had no suitable field data for the primary-creep stage) publishes in Cold Regions Science and Technology and does not engage with the firn-rheology calibration problem at all. So each community holds half the pair. || PREMISES VERIFIED: I downloaded and text-extracted the full PDF of the single most on-point modern document — Arrizabalaga-Iriarte et al., 'Firn densification in two dimensions: modelling the collapse of snow caves and enhanced densification in ice-stream shear margins', Journal of Glaciology 71, e61, doi:10.1017/jog.2025.6 — and read its complete reference list. Verbatim from the body: 'In an attempt to further characterize the model dependence on k, we searched for alternative validation experiments that involve near-surface (low-density) firn, since the choice of k affects compressibility the most there. We found that the observed collapse of a cylindrical subsurface tunnel, constructed at the NEEM ice core site, is well-suited for this purpose.' And: 'the tunnel collapse rate was tracked for 3 years after its construction.' The paper also states its global best-fit k 'might not be strictly applicable across all sites' and that 'The underestimation of density at depth is present in all the sites modeled.' Keyword counts over the extracted text: 'Camp Century' = 2, 'CRREL' = 1, 'Fistclench' = 0, 'SIPRE' = 0, 'Mellor' = 0, 'Abele' = 0, 'Byrd' = 0. Both Camp Century hits and the single CRREL hit are the SAME reference, cited only for a construction technique, not for data: 'Clark E (1965) Camp Century evolution of concept and history of design construction and performance. Technical Report 174, CRREL', invoked as 'the Camp Century snow-blowing casting technique (Clark, 1965)'. The nearest thing to prior cavity work in the bibliography is Brondex et al. 2020 (Dome C snow cave vs rigid container, a modelling study). No instrumented closure dataset from the 1950s–60s appears anywhere in the reference list. On the old side I confirmed via ERDC-Library and DTIC records that CRREL TR 121 (AD0430148), Waterhouse, Tobiasson & Scott, May 1963, 'Camp Century movement record', describes '18 additional cross section measurement stations and 29 movement recording Helipots' installed after the 1959–1960 trenches and frames its purpose as defining the 'useful life' of undersnow facilities; and that AD0407076, 'Byrd Station snow tunnels — wall clearing study', reports closure rates in most of the tunnels. I did NOT obtain the full text of TR 121 (apps.dtic.mil returned HTTP 403 for the PDF), so the scout's first job is to pull it from ERDC-Library and confirm the tabulated rates. || COHERENCE: Regime matches. Camp Century trenches sat under roughly 2-10 m of firn at a mean annual temperature near -24 C; NEEM is near -29 C, so the activation-energy correction between them is a factor of order 1.5, not orders of magnitude. Overburden at 5-10 m depth in firn of 400-600 kg/m3 gives 0.02-0.06 MPa, with modest stress concentration at the cavity crown — squarely in the low-stress, non-linear-viscous creep regime the 2-D rheology is written for, and well below any pressure-melting or brittle-fracture threshold. Densities of 0.40-0.60 Mg/m3 correspond to relative density 0.44-0.65, i.e. exactly the sub-0.8 range where the paper says sensitivity to k is largest. The reported closure of order 0.3 m/yr on a span of order 5 m is a bulk strain rate of order 6 percent per year, about 2e-9 per second — the same order as published firn compaction strain rates, so the numbers are self-consistent rather than off by decades. The one genuine confound is thermal, not mechanical: buried heat sources raise local creep rates, which is why the heated reaches must be excluded. || HOW TO CHECK: Falsifiable in both directions and cheap. (a) Bibliographic claim: anyone can re-extract the 2025 Journal of Glaciology reference list and check whether any 1950s-60s instrumented closure dataset is cited; if one is, the target dies immediately. (b) Data claim: pull CRREL TR 121 from ERDC-Library and check whether the cross-section stations yield closure rate versus depth, density, span and temperature. If it turns out to be narrative only, with no tables, the target dies. (c) Scientific payoff claim: digitise the unheated reaches, fit k by the same inversion the 2025 paper uses on the NEEM trench, and compare. A k that lands inside the paper's own 100-500 bracket and is consistent across several independent sites and spans would do what the authors say their single warm-summer-confounded NEEM case cannot. A k that is wildly inconsistent across sites would instead be evidence that the compressible-viscous form is wrong at low density, which is also a publishable result.
targets.domain: Submarine, polar and remote-station engineering where long unattended operation forced solutions since abandoned

targets.problem: The mercury-cell chlor-alkali industry spent roughly eighty years quantifying ONE thing with safety-critical precision: how to keep an alkali metal dissolved in a liquid-metal cathode in contact with a protic medium at extreme cathodic potential WITHOUT losing the current to hydrogen. That corpus contains numerical tolerance specifications for the specific trace transition metals that destroy hydrogen overvoltage on mercury and amalgams — vanadium, molybdenum, chromium, manganese, tungsten, iron, nickel, cobalt, sulfide, and graphite particulate — at the ~10 ppb level, plus the diagnostic signature of poisoning and the remedies. The modern lithium- and calcium-mediated electrochemical ammonia synthesis field is fighting exactly this failure mode: parasitic hydrogen evolution at an alkali-metal/protic-additive interface, with notoriously poor reproducibility between labs, and it frames the problem entirely in terms of SEI engineering, ion solvation, proton-shuttle (ethanol) concentration, and trace water. It routinely uses MOLYBDENUM foil working electrodes and steel hardware — molybdenum being one of the canonical hydrogen-overvoltage poisons in the mercury-cell literature. Task for the comb: recover the quantitative poison list and its concentration thresholds from the chlor-alkali corpus, map it onto the reagent and hardware inventory of Li-mediated nitrogen reduction (THF, LiClO4/LiBF4 salts, ethanol, stainless/Mo electrodes, N2 feed lines), and test whether ppb-level transition-metal contamination accounts for a measurable share of the field's hydrogen-evolution losses and its lab-to-lab irreproducibility.
targets.notes: B-terms (modern -> OLD vocabulary for the same quantity): HER selectivity / Faradaic efficiency loss -> 'hydrogen in chlorine', 'current efficiency loss', 'cell gassing'; catalyst poisoning -> 'depolarisation of the cathode', 'loss of hydrogen overvoltage', 'brine impurity'; electrolyte purity spec -> 'brine specification', 'brine purification' (dechlorination, resaturation, chemical/physical purification, pH 4.5-5.5); liquid-metal cathode -> 'mercury cathode', 'amalgam', 'butterfly' and 'thick amalgam' operation; parasitic self-discharge of plated alkali metal -> 'amalgam decomposition'. WHERE TO DIG: the Chlorine Bicentennial Symposium volume (Electrochemical Society, 1974); Journal of Applied Electrochemistry and Electrochimica Acta, 1965-1990; F. Hine, 'Electrode Processes and Electrochemical Engineering' (1985); Schmittinger's 'Chlorine' monograph; Euro Chlor and Chlorine Institute technical/GEST reports (trade grey literature, NOT journals); UNIDO process monographs; Soviet work in Elektrokhimiya and Zhurnal Prikladnoi Khimii (language barrier — a second severance layer); and the mercury-cell patent literature, which carries the numbers in its background sections. CONFIRMED ANCHOR I actually saw (Canadian patent CA 1122923, background section, read via search result): 'Quantities varying from 0.3 to 0.01% of impurities such as calcium, magnesium and iron are usually present in salt while other heavy metals like Cr, V, Mo, Mn are often present in a concentration of about 0.01 ppm. These impurities must be carefully removed from the brine since quantities higher than 0.01 ppm in the brine can cause hydrogen to evolve at the mercury cathode after an extended period of time.' That is the orphaned 10-ppb threshold, in the old idiom. TRAPS TO AVOID: (1) The Li-NRR field DOES have a rigorous-protocol / contamination literature (post-2019, after the Andersen-Chorkendorff protocol) — but it is about NITROGEN-CONTAINING contaminants (NOx, adventitious NH3, nitrate in membranes) producing FALSE POSITIVES, not about transition metals catalyzing HER. Do not let a scout see the word 'impurity' in that literature and declare the premise false; read what the contaminant actually is. (2) Do not propose mercury itself as a cathode — this is about the DATA, not the material. (3) Do not overclaim that the chlor-alkali corpus is unknown to electrochemists generally; it is standard industrial electrochemistry. The claim is specifically that its numerical poison thresholds have not been imported into the alkali-metal-mediated nitrogen-reduction field. || CORE PREMISE: The chlor-alkali mercury-cell literature's quantitative hydrogen-overvoltage poison thresholds (ppb-level specifications for V, Mo, Cr, Mn and related species on a liquid alkali-metal-bearing cathode in a protic medium) are absent from the alkali-metal-mediated electrochemical ammonia-synthesis literature, which attributes its hydrogen-evolution losses and irreproducibility to SEI composition, solvation and water content and has never specified or assayed trace transition-metal purity for this purpose. || DISCONTINUITY: Regulatory extinction of an entire electrochemical technology, on two dated instruments. (1) Commission Implementing Decision 2013/732/EU of 9 DECEMBER 2013 established the BAT conclusions for chlor-alkali production under the Industrial Emissions Directive, declaring mercury-cell operation not BAT; under the IED, BAT conclusions become binding four years after publication, giving a hard compliance date of 11 DECEMBER 2017. (2) Regulation (EU) 2017/852 on mercury bans chlor-alkali production using mercury as an electrode from 11 DECEMBER 2017. European producers converted or dismantled their mercury facilities to meet it. In parallel the Minamata Convention (adopted 10 October 2013, in force 16 August 2017) phases out mercury chlor-alkali globally, and the surviving plants moved to membrane technology or to non-OECD jurisdictions. Supporting earlier precedent in the same domain: the last North American ammonia-soda plant, Allied Chemical's works at Solvay, New York, closed in 1985-86, after which 'there have been no Solvay-based plants operating in North America' — the same pattern of an entire process-chemistry community vanishing from the domestic literature. || GAP MECHANISM: Not bibliographic. (a) DOCUMENTED COMMERCIAL AND LEGAL ABANDONMENT on a fixed date: after 11 December 2017 nobody in the EU could legally operate a mercury cell, so the research community that owned liquid-metal-cathode hydrogen-overvoltage expertise ceased to exist as a going concern and its training pipeline closed. The knowledge was never a journal-resident body in the first place — it lived in trade grey literature (Euro Chlor/Chlorine Institute reports), plant operating specifications, and patent background sections, all of which die with the industry. (b) VOCABULARY SPLIT FOR THE SAME PHYSICAL QUANTITY: 'loss of hydrogen overvoltage from 10-ppb vanadium in the brine' and 'HER Faradaic efficiency loss on the working electrode' are the same measurement; no keyword path connects them, and 'brine' guarantees that a non-aqueous electrochemist's search never reaches it. (c) SCOPE CONDITION CHANGED: chlor-alkali engineers cared about hydrogen because it made explosive mixtures with chlorine and cost current efficiency at industrial scale; Li-NRR researchers care about hydrogen because it is a competing reaction at bench scale. Same physics, non-overlapping motivation, non-overlapping journals, and a 2017 legal wall between the two communities. || PREMISES VERIFIED: Europe PMC boolean searches, run 2026-10-21: ('electrolyte purity' AND 'lithium-mediated' AND 'ammonia') = 0 hits. ('mercury cell' AND 'cathode poisoning') = 0 hits. ('lithium-mediated' AND 'amalgam') = 1 hit, which is a review of metal-modulated platelet activation and coagulation — entirely irrelevant. ('sodium amalgam' AND 'electrosynthesis') = 1 hit, a 2020 Chem Rev on molecular N2-to-NH3 catalysis, where 'amalgam' refers to sodium amalgam as a chemical reductant for molecular complexes, NOT to cathode overvoltage. ('chlor-alkali' AND 'nitrogen reduction') = 6 hits, all generic electrocatalysis or techno-economic reviews that mention chlor-alkali only as a scale comparator. By contrast ('molybdenum' AND 'lithium-mediated' AND 'ammonia') = 11 hits of live, current work — 'The Role of Ethanol in Lithium-Mediated Nitrogen Reduction' (JACS 2025), 'A carbon cathode for lithium mediated electrochemical ammonia synthesis' (Energy Environ Sci 2025), 'The origin of overpotential in lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction' (Faraday Discuss 2023), 'The role of ion solvation in lithium mediated nitrogen reduction' (J Mater Chem A 2023), 'Towards understanding of electrolyte degradation in lithium-mediated non-aqueous electrochemical...' (RSC Adv 2021) — confirming an active field whose stated causal vocabulary for its losses is ethanol/proton-shuttle, SEI, ion solvation and electrolyte degradation, with no trace-transition-metal purity axis. A targeted web search for the Li-mediated-NRR literature against mercury-cathode/chlor-alkali precedent returned, verbatim in the result summary, 'No results addressed this.' On the old side, the poison threshold is real and quantitative: CA 1122923's background gives Cr, V, Mo, Mn at ~0.01 ppm in salt and states that above 0.01 ppm in the brine they 'can cause hydrogen to evolve at the mercury cathode'. CAVEATS the scout must close FIRST: (i) Europe PMC under-indexes Nature, Science, Joule, Nature Catalysis, ACS Energy Letters and Nature Energy, where much flagship Li-NRR work appears — re-run the co-occurrence in Scopus/WoS before spending budget. (ii) I did NOT open the full reference list of a flagship Li-NRR paper; do that (Suryanto et al. Science 2021; Du et al. Nature 2023; the Faraday Discussions 2023 overpotential paper) and grep for chlor-alkali, amalgam, mercury cathode, overvoltage, Hine, Euro Chlor. (iii) The 0.01 ppm figure is from a single patent's background section and must be corroborated against Journal of Applied Electrochemistry or Euro Chlor primary sources before it is used as a number. || COHERENCE: Coherent, with one scope difference stated honestly. SIGN CHECK — this is the critical one and it passes: both fields want hydrogen evolution SUPPRESSED, and in both a trace transition-metal deposit LOWERS the hydrogen overpotential and thus INCREASES the parasitic hydrogen current. Same sign, same direction, same desired outcome; no sign inversion is required to make the bridge work. REGIME: the chlor-alkali data are aqueous, on mercury, with ~0.2-0.5 wt% sodium in amalgam, at roughly 60-80 C, 1 atm, a few kA/m2. Li-mediated NRR is non-aqueous (THF with ethanol or trace water as the proton shuttle), plating lithium on steel, Mo or carbon, at ambient temperature, 1-20 bar N2, a few mA/cm2, around -3 to -4 V versus a lithium-plating reference (one reported figure: approximately -3.59 V vs RHE at 6.5% Faradaic efficiency in LiClO4/ethanol/THF). The media and the current densities DIFFER — I am not claiming the numerical 10-ppb threshold transfers unchanged, and a scout that claims so should be corrected. What transfers is (1) the IDENTITY and RANKING of the poison species, which is set by their exchange-current density for hydrogen and is a property of the metal, not of the solvent, and (2) the finding that the relevant concentration scale is ppb and not ppm — i.e. that a contamination level nobody in the modern field currently specifies or measures is sufficient to change the result. ARITHMETIC: 0.01 ppm is 10 ug/L, which is roughly 10^-7 M for a mid-transition metal; routine ICP-MS detection limits for V, Mo and Cr are in the ng/L range, so the assay is three to four orders of magnitude inside instrument capability. Deliberate dosing at 1, 10 and 100 ppb into a THF/LiClO4 electrolyte is trivially preparable. Nothing here requires high pressure, cryogenics, or an extrapolation outside measured regimes. || HOW TO CHECK: Verifiable in stages, cheapest first. (a) KILL TEST: Scopus/WoS co-occurrence on the BARE concepts, no application words — ('hydrogen overvoltage' OR 'hydrogen overpotential' OR 'cathode depolarisation') AND ('amalgam' OR 'mercury cathode') AND ('nitrogen reduction' OR 'ammonia synthesis'); and separately, whether ANY alkali-metal-mediated-NRR paper specifies a transition-metal purity limit for its electrolyte. If one does, the target is dead. (b) REFERENCE-LIST TEST: grep the full reference lists of the three flagship Li-mediated-NRR papers and of the two most recent reviews for any chlor-alkali, amalgam, or mercury-cathode citation. (c) ASSAY TEST, cheap and decisive, needs no new electrochemistry: ICP-MS a batch each of the exact reagents the field uses — battery-grade THF, LiClO4 and LiBF4, anhydrous ethanol — plus a leachate from a stainless-steel cell body and from Mo foil, and ask whether V, Mo, Cr, Mn, Fe, Ni or Co are present above 10 ppb. A positive assay alone makes the hypothesis live and is publishable as a methods note. (d) CAUSAL TEST: dose a standard Li-mediated NRR cell at 1, 10 and 100 ppb of each poison and measure ammonia Faradaic efficiency and the hydrogen partial current against an undosed control. A monotonic efficiency decline over that range would explain a real, acknowledged reproducibility problem; a flat response falsifies the target outright.
targets.domain: Process industries that relocated offshore, leaving their domestic technical literature orphaned (textiles, tanning, heavy chemicals, shipbuilding)

targets.problem: Modern thermal-dose safety limits for whole-body heating in humans (the CEM43 framework used for MRI RF exposure limits, MR-guided focused ultrasound, and systemic/whole-body hyperthermia oncology) rest almost entirely on animal and single-acute-exposure local-heating data. The 1930s-40s artificial-fever-therapy literature (Kettering Hypertherm and similar radiant/diathermy cabinets, used for neurosyphilis, gonococcal arthritis/salpingitis, and other infections) delivered many thousands of deliberately induced, instrumented whole-body hyperpyrexia sessions to humans, with continuously recorded rectal temperature-time curves, prescribed plateau temperatures, session durations, cumulative session counts per patient, and tabulated complications, terminations and deaths. That is almost certainly the largest human whole-body thermal dose-toxicity dataset ever assembled. Task: extract temperature-time histories and adverse-event data from the 1931-1945 fever-therapy corpus, convert each session to CEM43 using the standard Sapareto-Dewey formulation, and build an empirical human whole-body CEM43 vs. toxicity curve to test the thresholds now in force.
targets.notes: B-terms / old vocabulary: 'artificial fever', 'fever therapy', 'hyperpyrexia', 'pyretotherapy', 'pyrotherapy', 'electropyrexia', 'physical hyperthermy', 'hypertherm', 'fever cabinet', 'inductothermy', 'short-wave diathermy fever'. The old corpus never says 'thermal dose', 'CEM43', 'thermal isoeffect dose', or 'cumulative equivalent minutes' — those are 1984+ (Sapareto & Dewey). It says 'temperature level' in degrees F and 'duration of fever' in hours, often as 'hours at 106 F'. Dig in: JAMA, Archives of Physical Therapy, Radiology, Am J Syphilis Gonorrhea & Venereal Diseases, Am J Psychiatry, Cleveland Clinic Quarterly, Arch Neurol Psychiatry, 1931-1945; the Univ. of Minnesota Hospitals Fever Therapy Department reports; Bauer & Cecil 1938 (US Venereal Disease Division reprint, gonorrheal complications via Kettering hypertherm); Zeiter's physical-hyperpyrexia review in Cleveland Clinic Quarterly 4(2):98; the 1939 Radiology review of fever therapy in gonococcal infection; a 1939 Kettering-hypertherm leprosy series (18 patients, 164 sessions, 15 sessions terminated early for complications). Also search Spanish/Portuguese (Arquivos de Neuro-Psiquiatria carried 'eletropirexia' papers into 1946) and German ('Fiebertherapie', 'Hyperthermiebehandlung'). TRAPS: (a) do not conflate malariotherapy (Wagner-Jauregg, 1917) with cabinet therapy — malaria fever was uninstrumented and the temperature-time curve is unusable; restrict to physically induced fever where rectal temperature was charted. (b) Many papers report the PRESCRIBED plateau, not the achieved curve; only sessions with actual charts or stated time-above-temperature are usable. (c) Deaths in these series are often from the underlying disease (pneumonia, carcinoma) — the extraction must separate heat-attributable events (circulatory collapse, hepatic necrosis, renal shutdown, CNS sequelae, burns from the cabinet) from intercurrent mortality. (d) Thermometry was mercury rectal, sampling every 15-30 min; quantify that uncertainty rather than ignoring it. (e) Patients were young adults with syphilis/gonorrhea — selected for cardiac fitness, which biases the toxicity curve optimistically; this is a scope condition to state, not to hide. || CORE PREMISE: The published human whole-body hyperpyrexia sessions of 1931-1945 routinely delivered cumulative thermal doses in the ~15-90 CEM43 range with documented, quantified complication rates, and no modern thermal-dose guidance document derives its human limits from that corpus. || DISCONTINUITY: Chemotherapeutic displacement of the exact indications fever cabinets existed to treat, in two dated steps: sulfanilamide for gonococcal infection (Dees & Colston, Lancet 1937) removed the highest-volume fever-therapy indication within about two years; then Mahoney, Arnold & Harris's penicillin treatment of syphilis (Am J Public Health 33:1387, 1943) removed neurosyphilis, the remaining indication. Fever-therapy departments and the commercial cabinet trade (the Kettering Hypertherm line, developed with Charles F. Kettering around 1931-33) were gone by the late 1940s, and the whole literature stops. When whole-body hyperthermia was reinvented from the 1970s onward it came out of radiation oncology and cell-culture thermal biology (Sapareto & Dewey 1984), a different discipline with a different journal set, and it rebuilt its dose metric from rodent and in-vitro isoeffect data rather than from the abandoned clinical corpus. || GAP MECHANISM: Not a citation-count gap: it is a vocabulary split for the identical physical quantity plus total institutional extinction of the originating specialty. The old corpus expresses whole-body thermal exposure as 'hours at 106 F' inside infectious-disease, psychiatry and physical-therapy journals; the modern corpus expresses the same quantity as CEM43 inside radiology, MR safety and oncology journals. There is no shared index term, no shared journal, and no surviving practitioner lineage, because the specialty was abolished by antibiotics rather than absorbed. Confirmed asymmetry: van Rhoon et al., Eur Radiol 2013;23(8):2215-2227, the paper whose thresholds underpin MR RF exposure guidance, has exactly ONE pre-1960 reference in its entire list — Moritz & Henriques, Am J Pathol 1947;23:695-720, a contact-burn study — and no fever-therapy, pyrotherapy or artificial-fever reference at all. || PREMISES VERIFIED: I fetched the full text of van Rhoon et al. 2013 (PMC3799975) and read its reference list. Only one entry predates 1960 (ref. 27, Moritz & Henriques 1947, contact thermal burns). No 1930s-40s clinical fever-therapy, pyrotherapy, artificial-fever or whole-body hyperthermia human study appears. The paper states its thresholds come from two prior reviews (Dewhirst et al.; Yarmolenko et al.), that 'Data on time-temperature thresholds for thermal damage of healthy tissue were compiled in extensive reviews', that 'Collectively, the reviews gathered data for 11 species', and explicitly concedes 'a paucity of such data in humans'. Companion confirmation from the Dewhirst review: 'there are virtually no data that directly relate to the thermal sensitivity of human tissues, so guidelines built on this data need significant caution'; and from Yarmolenko et al. (Int J Hyperthermia 2011;27(4):320-343): 'All of the studies reported are for single acute thermal exposures', with a noted 'critical lack of publications examining effects of chronic thermal exposures' and 'few in vivo papers examining the type and extent of damage in the lower temperature range ... (e.g. 39-42 degrees C)' — which is precisely the fever-therapy regime. Separately verified that the old corpus exists in quantified form: a University of Minnesota Hospitals fever-therapy department report states 'The Fever Therapy Department of the University of Minnesota Hospitals began to function February 25, 1936. Since the opening date 26 months ago, 98 patients have been given a total of 646 artificial fever treatments. There have been no untoward sequellae, no important complications, and no deaths.' A 1946 Arquivos de Neuro-Psiquiatria cabinet series reports sessions averaging 8 hours, 10 sessions per patient, with an operating range of '39,5 C (103 F) and a little above 41 C (105,8 F)'. NOT YET VERIFIED by me, flagged for the scout: the exact Dees & Colston 1937 and Mahoney 1943 citation strings, the total national volume of fever-therapy sessions, and whether any 2015-2026 hyperthermia or MR-safety paper or granted patent has already mined this corpus — run that kill-check first (OpenAlex: search=artificial fever therapy thermal dose; and a Google Patents search on whole-body hyperthermia thermal dose prior art). || COHERENCE: Arithmetic checks and is the heart of the target. CEM43 = t * R^(43-T) with R = 0.25 below 43 C. A documented 5-hour plateau at 41.5 C gives 0.25^1.5 = 0.125, so 300 min * 0.125 = 37.5 CEM43. Five hours at 41.0 C gives 0.25^2 = 0.0625, i.e. 18.8 CEM43. Six hours at 42.0 C gives 0.25^1 = 0.25, i.e. 90 CEM43 in a single session. Against this, van Rhoon's proposed limits are TD < 9 CEM43 for persons with intact thermoregulation under controlled conditions and < 2 CEM43 uncontrolled, with 10 CEM43 cited as the highest value below which no thermal damage was observed in large animals and humans. So the 1930s cabinets delivered roughly 2x to 10x the modern 'no-damage' ceiling, whole-body, repeatedly (about 10 sessions per patient course), to thousands of humans whose outcomes were written down. The temperature regime is ordinary clinical hyperpyrexia at 1 atm with intact perfusion — no exotic pressure or phase-change assumption is involved, and 41-42 C survivable whole-body plateaus are well attested. The cumulative-dose question (does CEM43 add across sessions days apart, given thermotolerance induction?) is itself one of the things the old corpus can answer and the modern corpus admits it cannot. || HOW TO CHECK: Fully verifiable from digitized public-domain and open-access sources, no new experiment required. (1) Assemble sessions from the 1931-1945 corpus via Internet Archive, HathiTrust, NLM Digital Collections (collections.nlm.nih.gov has OCR of the relevant monographs), SciELO for the Brazilian electropyrexia papers, and PMC's scanned historical journal holdings. (2) Digitize each published temperature-time chart, numerically integrate CEM43 with R = 0.25 (<43 C) and report sensitivity to R = 0.2-0.33. (3) Tabulate heat-attributable complications and deaths per session and per cumulative dose, with denominators. (4) Fit and publish an empirical human whole-body CEM43-vs-toxicity curve with confidence bounds, and state where it agrees or disagrees with the 9/10 CEM43 figures now used in MR safety guidance. Falsifiers that would kill the target outright: the reconstructed doses land below ~10 CEM43 (then there is no tension to report); the surviving papers report prescribed rather than achieved temperatures too often to integrate; or a 2015-2026 paper or patent already published this reconstruction.

targets.problem: Whether and how to cool a febrile patient with systemic infection is live and unresolved (Schortgen 2012 was neutral-to-ambiguous; SEPSISCOOL II, NCT04494074, 820 patients, 60-day mortality, is still awaited). Modern trials use slow surface cooling — water-circulating pads, blankets, cooled air — targeting normothermia over hours, and achieve roughly 0.5-1 C over many hours with high rates of shivering countermeasure use. The human dose-response and safety data for RAPID intermittent immersion cooling against an actively elevated hypothalamic set-point does not exist in the modern literature. It does exist, at enormous scale, in the 1890-1920 'water treatment' / Brand-bath literature for typhoid fever: a protocolized intervention (immersion at roughly 18-21 C for 15-20 minutes, repeated as often as every three hours, for weeks) applied to tens of thousands of bacteremic patients, with per-bath pre/post temperature readings, pulse and respiration, recorded reactions (rigor, collapse, delirium, cyanosis), and hospital-series mortality denominators. Task: recover from that corpus the achieved cooling rate per bath as a function of water temperature, immersion duration and starting core temperature, the rebound-rate after exit, and the per-bath adverse-event rate — then test whether modern slow surface cooling is simply underdosing, and whether rapid immersion in a bacteremic patient is as hemodynamically dangerous as current practice assumes.
targets.notes: B-terms / old vocabulary: 'the water treatment', 'the bath treatment', 'cold bathing', 'the Brand bath', 'Brand-Ziemssen method', 'tubbing', 'cold tub', 'hydrotherapy', 'balneotherapy', 'the cold pack', 'sponging', 'graduated bath'; mortality is given as 'the death-rate'. The old corpus never says 'targeted temperature management', 'external cooling', 'cooling rate C/min', 'thermoregulatory set-point' or 'shivering thermogenesis'. Dig in: BMJ, Lancet, JAMA, Boston Med Surg J, Am J Med Sci, Trans Assoc Am Physicians, Bull Johns Hopkins Hosp, 1890-1925; Osler's typhoid chapters; the German Munich military hospital series; NLM Digital Collections OCR (several relevant monographs are at collections.nlm.nih.gov, e.g. nlm:nlmuid-101484399-bk and nlm:nlmuid-101484379-bk) and Internet Archive. Also look for the WWI-era army typhoid ward reports. TRAPS: (a) do NOT make the target about whether the Brand bath reduced mortality — the comparisons are advocate-reported, non-randomized, span different hospitals and eras, and were contested at the time (one German review cited '7 per cent, with expectant, and of 8 per cent, with the water treatment at Hamburg'; a Bellevue series reported 33 per cent with iced baths). That question is unanswerable from this corpus and a scout who chases it will burn its budget. The recoverable payload is PHYSIOLOGICAL DOSE-RESPONSE AND PER-EXPOSURE SAFETY, where each bath is its own observation and the mortality confounding is irrelevant. (b) Many sources are OCR scans with garbled numerals — every extracted figure must be read against the page image. (c) Distinguish immersion from sponging and from the cold pack; they are different thermal doses and the literature uses the words loosely. (d) Do not import the exertional-heat-stroke target cooling rate (>=0.155 C/min) as a benchmark without noting that it was derived under a normal set-point. || CORE PREMISE: The modern cold-water-immersion cooling-rate literature is entirely about exertional/classic heat illness, in which the hypothalamic set-point is NORMAL and the body is passively overloaded; no modern dataset gives immersion cooling kinetics or per-exposure adverse-event rates for fever, where the set-point is RAISED and active thermogenesis opposes the cooling — and the 1890-1920 typhoid hydrotherapy corpus is the only large human dataset of exactly that. || DISCONTINUITY: Two dated severances, both documented. First, pharmacological displacement: the salicylate/antipyrine 'antipyretic method' pushed hydrotherapy out of routine use in the 1900s-1910s — contemporary editorials record that the bath method 'has gradually fallen into disuse, having been displaced by the more convenient and less tiresome antipyretic method', i.e. the labour-intensive physical intervention lost to a pill, exactly the commercial/labour abandonment pattern. Second and decisive: chloramphenicol for typhoid (Woodward, Smadel and colleagues, Kuala Lumpur, reported 1948) abolished prolonged enteric fever as a managed weeks-long illness in high-income countries within a few years. The disease that generated the entire dataset ceased to exist as a ward problem, so the technique had no successor patient population and no successor specialty: hospital hydrotherapy departments were dissolved into the newly rebranded 'physical medicine' of the 1940s, which kept the modalities for musculoskeletal work and dropped antipyresis entirely. || GAP MECHANISM: Scope condition changed plus a vocabulary split for the same physical quantity. The intervention did not fail on the merits and was not refuted; its indication was eliminated. Critical care rebuilt body-temperature control from scratch in the 1990s-2000s out of post-cardiac-arrest targeted temperature management, whose devices and vocabulary (surface pads, intravascular catheters, 'TTM', 'CEM'-free C/min) carry no link to 'the bath treatment'. Meanwhile the one modern community that does measure immersion cooling kinetics in humans — sports medicine and military heat-illness research — works exclusively on exertional hyperthermia, a DIFFERENT regulatory state, and therefore never had cause to look for fever-era data. So the two literatures are separated by both a disease that vanished and a discipline boundary that routes the relevant measurement to the wrong physiological model. || PREMISES VERIFIED: Co-occurrence check run on the bare concepts (cold water immersion + cooling rate + core temperature + febrile infection, with no history words): the entire returned modern corpus is exertional/classic heat illness — a 2015 meta-analysis of 19 studies ('Cold-water immersion increased the cooling rate by 0.03 C/min (95% CI = 0.03, 0.04 C/min) compared with passive recovery'), a 2020 systematic review of heat stroke first aid ('No single water temperature range was found to be associated with a quicker core temperature reduction than another (cold, colder or ice)'), a 2008 eight-man crossover finding 'Cooling in temperate water took only marginally longer than that in cold water', and a 2024 heat stroke guideline setting a target rate of 'at least 0.155 C/min' at 'very low' certainty. Nothing on fever of infectious origin, nothing on shivering dose-response in that setting, nothing historical. Separately checked the sepsis-cooling side: the field is Schortgen et al. 2012 (200 ventilated septic-shock patients, external cooling, primary vasopressor endpoint not met, exploratory day-14 mortality signal), Bernard 1997 ibuprofen, a 2013 meta-analysis of three RCTs totalling 320 participants, and the still-unreported SEPSISCOOL II (NCT04494074) — a very thin evidence base, consistent with an open question rather than a settled one. And confirmed the old corpus is quantitative: contemporary tabulations include cold bathing 'fairly strict' 1879-1889, 5,573 cases, 3.9% mortality; 'very strict', 1,223 cases, 1% mortality; Munich military hospital '2841 Expectant and bath combined, 1868-81, 12.2 per cent' vs '702 Strict cold baths and antipyretics, 1877-87, 7.6 per cent'; James C. Wilson, Philadelphia, 1890-1892, 226 cases, 5.3% mortality. NOT YET VERIFIED, flagged for the scout as the first kill-check: whether the Schortgen 2012 and SEPSISCOOL II reference lists cite any pre-1950 hydrotherapy source (open both and read them), and whether any 2015-2026 paper has already reconstructed per-bath cooling kinetics from this corpus. || COHERENCE: Arithmetic is coherent. Immersion at 18-21 C is in the mild-cold regime; measured whole-body immersion cooling rates are about 0.2-0.35 C/min in 2-14 C water and roughly 0.1 C/min at 20 C, so a 15-20 minute Brand bath predicts a core drop of about 1.5-2 C. Historical reports of 1.5-3 F (0.8-1.7 C) per bath sit just under that, which is exactly what an actively elevated set-point and intense shivering thermogenesis should produce — the discrepancy IS the signal being extracted, and its direction is the physiologically expected one, so the bridge needs the same sign, not the opposite. For contrast, Schortgen-style surface cooling achieves on the order of 0.5-1 C over several hours, i.e. roughly 5-10x less cooling power, which makes the underdosing hypothesis quantitatively live rather than rhetorical. Everything happens at 1 atm in water above 15 C with a conscious or delirious but spontaneously breathing patient: no incoherent pressure, phase or perfusion assumption. || HOW TO CHECK: No new experiment needed for the primary claim. (1) Extract, from digitized 1890-1925 sources, every reported bath with a stated water temperature, immersion duration, pre-bath and post-bath temperature, and recorded reaction; read each number against the page image because of OCR corruption. (2) Fit achieved delta-T per bath against water temperature, duration and starting core temperature, and extract the post-exit rebound slope, which the old charts record because temperature was taken continuously through the day. (3) Compute per-bath rates of collapse, rigor, syncope and cardiac events with explicit denominators — this is a safety dataset with tens of thousands of exposures that has no modern equivalent at any size. (4) Compare against the cooling rates and shivering rates reported in Schortgen 2012 and, when it reports, SEPSISCOOL II. Deliverable: an immersion cooling-rate and adverse-event prior for febrile bacteremic adults, directly usable to power or redesign a cooling-dose arm. Falsifiers: the old papers turn out to report only daily temperature curves rather than per-bath pre/post pairs (then the dose-response is unrecoverable and the target dies); adverse events are recorded only anecdotally with no denominators; or a modern sepsis-cooling paper already cites and uses this corpus.
