targets.problem: High-thermal-conductivity Si3N4 is now the substrate of choice for SiC/GaN power modules, bonded by active-metal brazing (AMB) to thick Cu. The structural-ceramics literature of the 1970s-90s measured the time-dependent strength loss of exactly this material class under sustained tensile stress in humid air and in water, and called it 'static fatigue' / 'delayed failure' / 'stress corrosion of ceramics', parameterized as the crack-velocity exponent n (and operationalized as SPT diagrams, proof-test lifetime diagrams, and NASA's CARES/Life reliability code). The power-electronics packaging literature measures the same underlying failure process but names it 'thermal cycling cycles-to-failure', 'damp heat / H3TRB-THB withstand hours' and 'B10 lifetime', and characterizes the ceramic itself only by fracture toughness K_IC and Weibull characteristic strength. Nobody converts between the two. The overlooked published answer: moisture-assisted subcritical-crack-growth (SCG) parameters for Y2O3/Al2O3-sintered Si3N4 at ambient-to-moderate temperature already exist in the old gas-turbine-era corpus, and combining them with published AMB residual-stress FEA gives a static-fatigue lifetime for the ceramic under the permanent Cu-mismatch tension at 85 C / 85 %RH — a number the 15-year automotive qualification currently does not produce.
targets.notes: B-TERMS / OLD VOCABULARY to search instead of the modern words: 'static fatigue', 'delayed failure', 'stress corrosion of ceramics', 'subcritical crack growth', 'crack velocity exponent N or n', 'stress-corrosion susceptibility parameter', 'dynamic fatigue (stressing-rate) method', 'strength-probability-time (SPT) diagram', 'proof-test lifetime diagram', 'fatigue limit in water-saturated air', 'ion exchange in the grain-boundary phase'. MODERN VOCABULARY on the other side: thermal cycling (TC), power cycling, H3TRB / HV-THB / damp heat, AQG-324, B10 lifetime, K_IC, Weibull modulus. WHERE TO DIG: Gulden, J. Am. Ceram. Soc. 59 (1976), 'Stress Corrosion of Si3N4' (time-dependent failure in water-saturated air, ~10% higher strength in dry air, mechanism = ion exchange in the glassy grain-boundary phase); 'Subcritical crack growth in Y-Al-Si-O-N glass', J. Non-Cryst. Solids (1998); the ESIS Si3N4 reference-material data (SCG at 22 C in deionized water, n about 50); the DOE/ORNL 'Ceramic Technology for Advanced Heat Engines' semiannual progress reports on OSTI and NASA Lewis TMs from AGT/ATTAP, which is where the n-values, proof-test methodology and CARES/Life live as grey literature. Also check Japanese-language and trade output from Kyocera, Toshiba Materials and MARUWA — they make AMB Si3N4 and may hold grade-specific data outside journals. TRAPS: (1) Do NOT use the plentiful 1000-1400 C SCG data (n about 13-22) as the bridge — that is glassy-phase viscous flow / cavitation, a different mechanism in the wrong regime, and using it is precisely the physically-incoherent-bridge failure mode. The bridge must be the ambient/low-temperature moisture-assisted data. (2) n about 50 for one ESIS reference grade means the effect is modest for that grade; the target lives or dies on grade-specific grain-boundary chemistry, and the aqueous-corrosion literature says Y2O3/Al2O3-bearing oxynitride boundaries are the LEAST hydrolytically stable — which is what high-conductivity AMB grades use. Report the grade dependence, do not average it away. (3) Si3N4 also shows genuine cyclic (not just time-dependent) crack growth; do not attribute all of it to SCG. (4) AMB residual tension is concentrated at the Cu plate edge/corner (where observed cracks actually initiate), so the SCG-stressed volume is small — handle this in the Weibull effective-volume term rather than using a bulk strength. (5) The modern blocking belief to attack explicitly: reviews state that covalent ceramics such as SiC and Si3N4 'are considered to be almost insensitive to SCG' — yet a sintered-Si3N4 patent states typical ceramics have n of 30-40 and are therefore 'to be qualified as subcritical crack growth, which would limit their practical life'. That contradiction inside the ceramics literature is the lever. || CORE PREMISE: No published work applies moisture-assisted subcritical-crack-growth (static-fatigue) lifetime analysis to the Si3N4 ceramic of an AMB power-module substrate under its permanent braze-induced tensile residual stress in damp heat; the AMB reliability literature treats the ceramic as a time-independent material characterized by K_IC and thermal-cycle counts, while the ambient-temperature moisture-assisted SCG data for this material class was published and then stranded. FALSIFIED IF: any paper, standard or vendor report computes an SCG/n-based lifetime (or an SPT/proof-test diagram) for an AMB or DBC Si3N4 substrate, or AQG-324/JEDEC guidance for ceramic substrates invokes a crack-velocity exponent. || DISCONTINUITY: Termination of the monolithic-structural-ceramic gas turbine programmes and the field's restart on a different material class: the DOE/NASA automotive ceramic turbine line AGT (1979-87) -> ATTAP, Advanced Turbine Technology Applications Project (1987-93/94, terminated), with Japan's 300 kW Ceramic Gas Turbine project under New Sunshine ending 1999; high-temperature structural ceramics then restarted on SiC/SiC ceramic matrix composites, abandoning the monolithic Si3N4 lifetime-prediction apparatus (n-values, SPT diagrams, CARES/Life). Si3N4 was then picked up ~20 years later by an entirely different community — power-electronics packaging — which arrived via Al2O3/AlN direct-bonded-copper practice and canonized its qualification toolkit in ECPE AQG-324 (first edition 2018), a thermal-cycling and damp-heat protocol inherited from substrates where the ceramic is not the life-limiting element. NOTE ON PROVENANCE: the scientific premises below were verified by search this session; the ATTAP/CGT/AQG-324 names and dates are from background knowledge and should be confirmed by the scout as step zero. || GAP MECHANISM: Three stacked mechanisms, none of them bibliographic. (1) Scope condition changed: the lifetime-prediction apparatus for monolithic Si3N4 was built to answer a high-temperature creep-and-oxidation question for turbine rotors; when that programme died the apparatus died with it, and the ambient moisture-assisted branch of it was the least-used part even then. (2) Toolkit imported from the wrong material class: power-electronics packaging qualifies substrates with thermal-cycle counts and damp-heat withstand hours, a protocol developed for Al2O3-DBC and organic laminates where the dielectric is not the fracture-critical element, so the ceramic enters the model only as K_IC and a Weibull strength — there is no slot in the model for a time-dependent crack-growth term, which means the quantity cannot be requested even if it is known. (3) A blocking belief: the modern consensus that covalent ceramics are 'almost insensitive to SCG' makes the search for n-values look unnecessary, so no one looks — while the same ceramics literature elsewhere reports n = 30-50 and warns this limits practical life. || PREMISES VERIFIED: WHAT I SEARCHED AND SAW. (a) Si3N4 AMB power-substrate reliability: a targeted search for AMB Si3N4 substrates under humidity/reverse bias, ceramic cracking under sustained stress, and lifetime prediction returned nothing of the kind. The on-point modern AMB papers (J. Eur. Ceram. Soc. 2017 and 2018, and a 2024 thermal-cycling simulation/fatigue-lifetime paper) characterize the ceramic only by fracture toughness and thermal-cycle crack counts: 0.30 mm Cu cracked under the plate corner after 100 cycles while 0.15 mm Cu survived 1000; residual bending strength fell to ~65% of as-received after 1000 cycles; a tougher 140 W/mK, ~10.5 MPa.m^0.5 grade showed almost no cracks. None gives an n-value, static-fatigue or SCG-based lifetime. H3TRB/HV-THB literature I checked discusses metallization corrosion and passivation/gate drift, not ceramic crack growth, and one study notes only in passing that thermo-mechanical stress 'might also promote the humidity induced degradation due to delamination or micro-cracks' — the hypothesis is stated and not pursued. (b) The old corpus EXISTS in the right regime, which is the fact the whole target rests on and which I checked last and specifically: Gulden 1976 (J. Am. Ceram. Soc. 59) found time-dependent failure of hot-pressed and reaction-sintered Si3N4 in water-saturated air with ~10% higher strength in dry air, attributed to ion exchange in the glassy grain-boundary phase; a J. Non-Cryst. Solids 1998 study reports subcritical crack growth in Y-Al-Si-O-N glass (the grain-boundary phase composition itself) immersed in deionized water; and the ESIS Si3N4 reference material shows SCG at 22 C in deionized water with an exponent of about 50. (c) Sign check on the bridge: the aqueous-corrosion literature states that resistance in hot aqueous solution is set by grain-boundary-phase stability and that Y2O3/Al2O3-containing compositions are the least stable — so water attacks the intergranular film that is also the crack path, and moisture ACCELERATES crack growth. Correct sign. (d) The blocking belief is real and quotable: a modern review states covalent ceramics such as SiC or Si3N4 'are considered to be almost insensitive to SCG', while a sintered-Si3N4 patent states typical ceramics have n of 30-40, 'apparently to be qualified as subcritical crack growth', which 'would limit their practical life'. (e) HONEST RESIDUAL RISK, stated rather than hidden: I did not find a compiled table of ambient-temperature humid-air n-values for modern Y2O3-sintered AMB-grade Si3N4; what I verified is that the mechanism and the measurement method are published for this material class in this regime. If the grey literature turns out to contain only n > 50 for all relevant grades, the quantitative consequence shrinks and the target should be reported as weak rather than forced. (f) KILLED BEFORE THIS ONE - do not regenerate: Protodyakonov f vs Bond work index (Chandar et al. and a ScienceDirect paper already regress BWI on the Protodyakonov index); ISO 3690 mercury-method diffusible hydrogen vs TCD/carrier-gas (the modern paper says comparability 'had already been investigated'); MacMullin number vs petrophysical formation factor (the on-point Li-ion paper literally writes 'the MacMullin number, also called the formation factor' and discusses Archie's law by name); pneumatic transmission-line lag vs soft robotics (an active fluid-power R-C-I transmission-line modelling literature, 2013-2017, never severed); PV soiling rate vs aerosol dry-deposition velocity (Sehmel-Hodgson and Slinn resistance models are already used and already measurement-model compared for solar collectors). Unverifiable, therefore not proposed: chlor-alkali membrane gas-permeation corpus vs electrolyzer hydrogen crossover; ACFTD-micron vs ISO 11171 micron(c) vs PSL-calibrated USP <788> counting; Soviet SNiP 'heat assimilation coefficient' vs thermal effusivity floor comfort. || HOW TO CHECK: Entirely desk-verifiable, no experiment needed, in three steps. (1) Harvest ambient-to-moderate-temperature moisture-assisted SCG parameters (n, and crack-velocity prefactor) for Y2O3/Al2O3-sintered Si3N4 from the stranded corpus: Gulden 1976 and its citing chain, the Y-Al-Si-O-N glass SCG paper, the ESIS reference-material dataset, and the DOE/ORNL Ceramic Technology for Advanced Heat Engines progress reports plus NASA AGT/ATTAP TMs on OSTI/NTRS. (2) Take peak tensile residual stress and Weibull strength parameters for AMB Si3N4 substrates straight from the published 2017-2024 FEA and bend-test papers already identified. (3) Run the SCG lifetime integral (or NASA's CARES/Life, which was built for exactly this and implements SCG natively) for 85 C/85 %RH and for 15-year service, and compare against the AQG-324 damp-heat duration. A positive result is a stated stress-margin number and a predicted grade ranking that the existing thermal-cycling data can be checked against retrospectively; a negative result (all relevant grades n >> 50, or peak tension far below the SCG threshold) kills it cleanly and cheaply. Decisive either way within a scout's budget.
targets.domain: Quantities that two fields measure under different names and never cross-calibrate

targets.problem: Single-phase immersion cooling of IT hardware qualifies coolants on dielectric STRENGTH and volume RESISTIVITY and treats flow-generated charge as nonexistent. The power-transformer insulating-liquid literature — same ASTM committee (D27), same fluid class — has a 45-year measured corpus showing that pumped low-conductivity hydrocarbon/ester liquids flowing over solid insulation generate streaming currents and kV-scale surface potentials, and that the hazard RISES as conductivity falls. Task: recover the measured electrostatic-charging-tendency (ECT) / streaming-current data for the exact fluid chemistries, velocities, filter media and solid-insulation pairings now used in immersion tanks, and show whether the OCP-specified resistivity floor is an anti-requirement.
targets.notes: B-terms and their OLD vocabulary: 'electrostatic charging tendency (ECT)' = ASTM D7620, IEC 61125; 'static electrification' = the 1979-1994 transformer term; 'streaming electrification' / 'flow electrification' = the current term; 'streaming current' and 'charge relaxation time' = Klinkenberg & van der Minne, Electrostatics in the Petroleum Industry, Elsevier 1958/1960 (pp. 62-64 is the turbulent-flow / double-layer passage); 'charge density in the laminar sublayer'; 'wall charge density p_w-infinity' and 'effective rate constant K' (2022 HAL paper hal-03641327); 'ECT reduction by benzotriazole (BTA), Irgamet 39, fullerene C60'. Where to dig: (1) EPRI TR-113441 (static electrification in power transformers) — it states that several 1979 reports from Japan indicated abnormally high-velocity oil flow could cause static electrification, that over a dozen U.S. failures have been associated with the problem since 1982, and that EPRI ran workshops in 1986, 1989, 1992 and 1994. (2) CIGRE WG D1 brochure 'D1-10916-2026 Flow electrification risk assessment of conventional and new alternative insulating liquids for power transformers' — key quote already seen: 'For conventional mineral oil, re-refined liquid and bio-based hydrocarbons, the results show that the accumulation of charges on the pressboard surface remains low with a limited hazard for transformer. This is probably related to the electrical conductivity of the oil, which increases with temperature and limits the potential rise within the pressboard.' That sentence is the whole bridge: conductivity is PROTECTIVE. Also: 'For ester Oil-BE, the flow electrification behaviour presents a reverse polarization with higher generating currents compared to mineral oils' — esters reverse polarity, so the mineral-oil fix (BTA) may be wrong-signed for ester immersion fluids. (3) Soton eprints 270856 (Mitchinson, EIM) for the oil/pressboard mechanism. (4) Zdanowski 2020-2022 Energies papers on ECT of Envirotemp FR3, Nycodiel 1255 and C60 nanofluids. (5) DTIC ADA092907 and ADA135751 for aviation-fuel measured charge accumulation below ~20 pS/m. TRAPS TO AVOID: (a) The flow-electrification literature itself is very much ALIVE (2022-2026) and it DOES cite Klinkenberg 1958 — do NOT frame this as 'nobody has measured streaming current' or 'these literatures are both dead'. The gap is one-directional: transformer->immersion, not immersion->transformer. (b) Do not claim immersion cooling ignores electrical risk generally — it does address dielectric breakdown and stray/leakage current; the specific omission is CHARGE GENERATION BY FLOW. (c) Liquid-hydrogen flow electrification is NOT an open gap (Int. J. Hydrogen Energy 2023 'Flow electrification characteristics of liquid hydrogen in pipe flow'; PRESLHY D4.1 names it as a studied knowledge gap) — do not drift there. (d) Aviation fuel is NOT an open gap either (Stadis 450 at 1-3 ppm, ASTM D2624, DEF STAN 91-091 50-600 pS/m). Use both only as the source of measured values. || CORE PREMISE: The modern immersion-cooling fluid qualification literature (OCP Immersion Requirements Rev 1/2.x, the ASTM D27.04 draft WK97110, and the 2022-2026 single-phase immersion review papers) prescribes NO measurement of flow-generated charge, while the transformer/petroleum electrostatics literature reports streaming currents and surface potentials, at the same fluid conductivities and comparable flow velocities, large enough to produce discharges — and the charge relaxation time of OCP-compliant fluids (tau = eps/sigma) exceeds the loop residence time by one to three orders of magnitude. || DISCONTINUITY: Two dated events, both documented. (1) 1979-1994, scope collapse: the static-electrification failure epidemic in large forced-oil-cooled power transformers — EPRI TR-113441 records 'several 1979 reports from Japan' tying high-velocity oil flow to static electrification and 'over a dozen U.S. failures ... since 1982', followed by EPRI workshops in 1986, 1989, 1992 and 1994. The problem was then closed out by velocity limits and benzotriazole additives, and the entire literature was scope-conditioned to 'oil/pressboard interface inside a large power transformer'. (2) 2021-2023, toolkit import from the wrong application class: the Open Compute Project Immersion Requirements documents (Rev 1, then Rev 2.0 and Rev 2.1, dated 2023-08-18) imported the ASTM D27 insulating-liquid electrical test battery — dielectric breakdown ASTM D1816, volume resistivity ASTM D1169, moisture ASTM D1533, permittivity and loss tangent — but omitted the one D27 method that addresses flow-generated charge, ASTM D7620 (ECT). The successor standard, ASTM WK97110 'New Specification for Single Phase Liquids used in Immersion Cooling of Data Centers', was initiated 2025-11-19 in subcommittee D27.04 and its published scope ('defining terminology, identifying liquid immersion specific parameters of importance, and containing requirements for liquid specifications') does not mention static charge. || GAP MECHANISM: A scope condition changed and a qualification toolkit was inherited across application classes. The ECT corpus was built to answer one question — will oil flowing at >0.5 m/s over cellulose pressboard inside a 500 kV transformer charge the pressboard enough to flash over — and once velocity limits plus BTA dosing answered it, the finding was filed under 'large power transformer design', not under 'properties of low-conductivity dielectric liquids in forced flow'. The immersion-cooling community then adopted the fluid class and most of its D27 test methods but not that one, because it reads 'dielectric fluid' as a synonym for 'electrically inert' and because its own engineering lineage is water/glycol liquid cooling, where sigma is ~10^-2 S/m and charge relaxation is instantaneous. The two literatures also use different names for the same physical quantity (static electrification / streaming electrification / flow electrification / electrostatic charging tendency / charging tendency / ECT), so keyword overlap between them is near zero even though the physics is identical. This is not a citation-count gap: it is a missing line in a qualification table, which is a falsifiable artifact. || PREMISES VERIFIED: Searched (a) the immersion-cooling side and (b) the electrification side separately, bare-concept, with no application words. (a) 'streaming current electrostatic charge generation dielectric coolant immersion cooling data center' returned only vendor and patent material; the search explicitly reported it 'didn't turn up anything on streaming current or electrostatic charge generation in immersion cooling'. A second, extended search ('immersion cooling dielectric fluid static electricity charge accumulation grounding risk electronics single-phase research') again returned no study on static charge in immersion tanks; the closest hits were (i) an industry report framing immersion electrical risk as 'stray currents' and 'dielectric breakdown', and (ii) US 8436246 (data-center refrigerant line ground isolation) which does state 'Many fluid handling operations can generate static electricity, especially if the fluid is a good dielectric' and 'This isolation between grounding schemes introduces static charge buildup in non-conductive sections of refrigerant hose assemblies' — i.e. the hazard is named in a cooling patent but absent from the fluid qualification literature. (b) The OCP fluid requirement rows were read from two independent secondary sources that agree: Engineered Fluids 'EC-120 OCP Compliance' (claims full compliance with 'the Open Compute Projects' fluids specifications requirements Revision 2.1 (2023-08-18)') and the GRC/ENEOS white paper, both listing dielectric strength '> 6 kV/mm' by ASTM D1816 at a 1 mm gap and volume resistivity '2.00 GOhm-m' (GRC: '> 2.0 GOhm-m for virgin fluids and > 0.2 GOhm-m over the fluid's life') by ASTM D1169, plus D1533 moisture, permittivity and loss tangent. No row on charge generation in either. The direct PDF returned HTTP 403 and api.openalex.org returned HTTP 429, so the OCP document text itself is NOT yet read first-hand — the scout must open https://www.opencompute.org/documents/ocp-acs-immersion-requirements-specification-1-pdf and the current Rev 2.x and confirm the absence of D7620/ECT before writing anything. ASTM WK97110 rationale quoted above was read from the ASTM work-item listing ('there is no industry standard for the liquids used in immersion cooling for data centers'; initiated 11-19-2025, subcommittee D27.04). On the counter-literature side, EPRI TR-113441 and the CIGRE D1-10916-2026 abstract were read as quoted above. I did NOT verify first-hand that any specific single-phase immersion review's reference list omits the electrification corpus — that is the scout's first job, and the most on-point document to open is the Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews / XJTU 'A comprehensive review of single-phase immersion cooling in data centres'. || HOW TO CHECK: Three cheap, decisive checks, in order. (1) DOCUMENT CHECK: open OCP Immersion Requirements Rev 1 and Rev 2.x and the ASTM WK97110 scope and grep for 'static', 'electrification', 'charging tendency', 'streaming', 'D7620', 'IEC 61125'. Absence is the finding; presence kills the target in ten minutes. Do the same on the ASTM D27 method index to confirm D7620 sits in the same committee that wrote D1816/D1169/D1533. (2) REFERENCE-LIST CHECK: open the most on-point modern review ('A comprehensive review of single-phase immersion cooling in data centres') and the Frontiers in Mechanical Engineering 2023 EV immersion-fluid properties paper, and read the reference lists for any transformer-electrification or petroleum-electrostatics citation. (3) NUMERICAL CHECK: pull measured streaming-current / ECT values (microcoulombs per cubic metre, or nanoamps of charging current) from the CIGRE D1-10916-2026 brochure, Zdanowski's Energies papers, and the 2022 HAL methodology paper (hal-03641327, which reports that 'the streaming current increases with the electrical conductivity, and with the oils viscosity'), then compute, for a representative immersion tank, the steady-state surface potential given a measured wall charge density, the published flow rate, the filter area, and tau from the fluid's own datasheet resistivity. If that potential exceeds a few kV the target is real and the deliverable is a one-page note: 'add ASTM D7620 to the immersion fluid qualification set, and specify a conductivity FLOOR, not only a resistivity floor.' The whole chain is paper-and-arithmetic; no experiment is required to establish the claim, though a benchtop loop with an electrometer on a grounded filter housing would confirm it directly.
targets.domain: Blocking beliefs: where a field states a material or effect is negligible, while another literature reports measured values large enough to matter

targets.problem: Plant-fibre (flax/hemp/jute) polymer composites are now being put into load-bearing or semi-structural service (small wind-turbine blades, automotive semi-structural panels, boat hulls, pultruded construction profiles) with creep/deflection allowables obtained from creep tests run in a CONSTANT environment, after moisture conditioning to equilibrium. Wood and paper science established between 1960 and roughly 2000 that cellulosic materials under load creep far faster while moisture content is CHANGING than at any constant moisture content (mechano-sorptive creep), and codified this into service-class deformation factors (Eurocode 5 k_def, up to 2.0 for service class 3; AS1720 j-factors; FPL creep work). TARGET QUESTION: do the already-published mechano-sorptive compliance coefficients and k_def-style factors supply the missing humidity-cycling creep design rule for plant-fibre composites, and quantitatively, by what factor does a constant-RH qualification protocol under-predict in-service creep of a flax laminate cycled 35-85% RH?
targets.notes: B-TERMS (modern side): flax/hemp/jute laminate creep compliance, deflection allowable, ASTM D2990, ASTM D5229, ASTM D570, CMH-17 B-basis, DNV-ST-0376 blade materials, IEC 61400-5. B-TERMS (old side, this is the vocabulary to search with): 'mechano-sorptive creep' / 'mechanosorptive', 'creep under varying moisture content', 'transient moisture creep', 'Armstrong and Kingston' (Nature, 1960), Ranta-Maunus (1975 onward), J.F. Hunt (USDA Forest Products Laboratory), Martensson, Hanhijarvi, 'deformation factor k_def' and 'service class' in EN 1995-1-1 (Eurocode 5), 'j2/j3 creep factors' in AS1720.1, ANC-18 (1944/1951). WHERE TO DIG: USDA Forest Products Laboratory reports (FPL-RP / FPL-GTR series, fpl.fs.usda.gov, full text free); Wood Science and Technology, Wood and Fiber Science (wfs.swst.org, open), Holzforschung; UK Forest Products Research Laboratory and Princes Risborough bulletins; TAPPI and paper-physics proceedings for the cellulose-fibre version; EverySpec for ANC-18 scans. TRAPS: (1) do NOT claim nobody has seen mechano-sorption in plant fibres - the single-elementary-fibre community has, and cites Armstrong and Kingston by name; the claim is about laminate-level allowables and the inherited protocol. (2) Do not conflate 'wet creep' (higher creep at high constant RH, well known in composites) with mechano-sorption (creep driven by the RATE of moisture change) - the whole target dies if that distinction is blurred. (3) Finish the two truncated reference lists (PMC10254661, PMC12299171) before writing 'absent'. (4) Secondary probe worth 30 minutes if the main one holds: wood science normalises every property to a reference 12% moisture content with published per-%MC adjustment equations and Hailwood-Horrobin sorption isotherms, while plant-fibre composite papers report properties at unspecified 'ambient' conditioning and then attribute the resulting 15-25% CoV to fibre variability - part of that scatter may be a conditioning artifact removable by the old normalisation, testable purely by meta-analysis of published datasets. || CORE PREMISE: The laminate-level durability/creep literature that will set allowables for plant-fibre composites does not use the wood/paper mechano-sorptive corpus: its moisture protocols condition specimens to equilibrium (ASTM D570 immersion, fixed-RH chambers) and its creep tests hold the environment constant, so the creep mechanism that dominates for cellulose under cycling humidity is invisible by construction to the protocol the field inherited from glass/carbon composites. || DISCONTINUITY: The aircraft structural-materials handbook system bifurcated around 1951 and the cellulose branch died. ANC-18 'Design of Wood Aircraft Structures' (Army-Navy-Civil Committee on Aircraft Design Criteria, June 1944; revised June 1951) carried the moisture-and-time mechanics of cellulose for airframes. Its sibling ANC-17 (plastics for aircraft) became MIL-HDBK-17 'Plastics for Flight Vehicles', which became MIL-HDBK-17 Part I Reinforced Plastics and then CMH-17 - the composite qualification lineage (coupon-level B-basis allowables, ASTM D5229 equilibrium conditioning, D2990 constant-environment creep) that plant-fibre composites inherit today. ANC-18's wood content was never carried over into that lineage; EverySpec lists both ANC-18 editions as inactive and an EASA rulemaking note states ANC-18 'is no longer a supported document' and that, lacking any alternative, EASA proposed citing ANC-18 directly in CS-23 guidance. Underlying physical cause: structural aircraft wood and flax-phenolic laminates (Gordon Aerolite, Duramold, Jicwood/Hydulignum) were displaced outright by aluminium between 1945 and 1955, so cellulose moisture-mechanics migrated into the building-code branch (NDS, AS1720, Eurocode 5) and its own journals, which composites engineers do not read. This is the same shape as the accepted 'fluidics killed by cheap silicon' survivor: an industry displaced, its qualification lineage abandoned, its physics corpus re-homed in a different profession. || GAP MECHANISM: Not a citation-count gap. Three concrete mechanisms: (1) PROTOCOL BLINDNESS - the inherited protocol conditions to equilibrium and then tests at fixed conditions, so no amount of testing inside the protocol can reveal a transient-moisture effect; the measurement is incapable, not merely absent. (2) VOCABULARY SPLIT FOR THE SAME PHYSICAL QUANTITY - wood science says 'mechano-sorptive creep', 'creep under varying moisture content', 'k_def', 'deformation factor', 'service class'; composites say 'hygrothermal creep', 'wet creep', 'moisture-assisted viscoelasticity', 'hot/wet knockdown'. A co-occurrence search in either vocabulary never retrieves the other corpus. (3) HANDBOOK/PROFESSION LINEAGE SPLIT (see discontinuity): the cellulose time-moisture knowledge sits in structural timber codes and in Wood Science and Technology / Wood and Fiber Science / Holzforschung, not in Composites Part A/B. || PREMISES VERIFIED: Co-occurrence check on bare concepts, no application words: (a) 'mechano-sorptive creep flax natural fibre composite cyclic humidity' returns only ELEMENTARY-FIBRE mechanics work (FEMTO-ST group on single hemp fibres; pulp-fibre work, 2015) - that niche DOES cite Armstrong and Kingston explicitly ('Armstrong and Kingston have shown that the creep of wood under transient humidity levels could be greatly accelerated over that at any constant moisture content') and reports 'more creep is also observed in cyclic humidity conditions than in a constant environment at the high-humidity' with a cycling-RATE threshold. So the bridge exists at single-fibre scale and the premise is restricted to laminate/qualification scale. (b) I opened the reference lists / full text of the two most on-point open-access modern reviews. 'Durability of Plant Fiber Composites for Structural Application: A Brief Review' (PMC10254661): none of mechano-sorptive, mechanosorptive, Armstrong, Kingston, Ranta-Maunus, Eurocode, k_def, or wood creep appear in the fetched text; creep is discussed only under constant conditioning ('Composites conditioned in 70 C and 85% relative humidity demonstrated higher creep deformation'); the only pre-1990 reference visible is Shen and Springer, J. Compos. Mater. 1976 (Fickian moisture absorption) - i.e. the field's historical anchor is the GLASS/EPOXY moisture model, exactly the inherited-protocol ancestor. (c) 'Effects of Moisture Absorption on the Mechanical and Fatigue Properties of Natural Fiber Composites: A Review' (PMC12299171): same term list absent in fetched text; moisture conditioning standard named is ASTM D570-22 immersion; no pre-1990 references visible. CAVEAT, stated plainly: both WebFetch reads were truncated (first ~100k of ~138k and ~160k characters), so the tail of each reference list was not read - the scout must re-check those tails before relying on 'absent'. (d) A further plant-fibre durability review states 'creep in PFCs has not received as much attention as water/moisture aging' and a 2026 review calls for coupled moisture/UV/fatigue testing while attributing scatter to fibre variability (CoV 15-25%) - i.e. the field is actively writing durability frameworks without this input. (e) KILLED CANDIDATE, for the record, so nobody re-runs it: I had a parallel target on hydrogen blending into PE/PVC gas mains vs town-gas-era grey literature. I extracted the full text of the AGA 2023 white paper 'Impacts of Hydrogen Blending on Gas Piping Materials' (62 pp) and it already cites the town-gas precedent AND live high-hydrogen networks - 'Hong Kong Gas Company has been using PE piping in their network since 1987 with a 46 - 52% hydrogen component', Singapore City Gas at 42-65% H2, Hawaii Gas SNG at 10-12% H2 since the early 1970s. Premise false; target discarded. || HOW TO CHECK: Two routes, the first needing no lab. (1) PURE RE-ANALYSIS: pull mechano-sorptive compliance coefficients (creep compliance increment per unit moisture-content change) from the wood/paper corpus, apply them to published constant-RH creep-compliance data for flax-epoxy and flax-PLA, and predict the under-prediction factor; then compare against the few published composite datasets that happen to have cycled humidity under load. A prediction that matches is a direct, citable transfer; a mismatch bounds the limits of transfer. (2) BENCH CHECK, cheap: one flax-epoxy coupon set in a programmable humidity chamber, 30% UTS, three arms - constant 35% RH, constant 85% RH, cycling 35<->85% RH with 6 h half-cycles - 1000 h, room temperature. The quantitative prediction to falsify: cycling creep strain exceeds the higher of the two constant-RH arms by a factor well above 1 (wood-derived estimate; state the number before running). Failure mode that would kill the target: cycling creep lands between the two constant arms.
targets.domain: Material classes adopted by a new industry that inherited a qualification protocol developed for a different material

targets.problem: Soil–crop model intercomparisons for sub-Saharan Africa are calibrated on a handful of post-1960 semi-arid/sub-humid sites and state outright that they need long-term experiments with soil C, N and root dynamics. Meanwhile the INÉAC network (Yangambi + ~20 satellite stations, Belgian Congo, 1933–1960) ran multi-year fertiliser, rotation, mulch/'couverture morte', corridor-system and FALLOW-LENGTH treatment arms on humid-tropical Ferralsols, with annual yields and soil organic matter reported in its own French-language monograph series. Task: locate the plot-level treatment × year yield and soil-organic-matter tables in the INÉAC corpus, pair them with the ALREADY-DIGITISED Yangambi 1930s–50s daily weather record, and test whether they constitute the first humid-tropical Congo-basin calibration/validation set for RothC, Century/DayCent, DSSAT-CENTURY and the APSIM/STICS family — in particular for fallow-length recovery of SOC and yield, which no modern African LTE has an arm for.
targets.notes: B-terms in the OLD vocabulary (search these, not modern terms): assolement; jachère forestière / jachère herbeuse; essais d'engrais / essais de fumure; paillage; couverture morte; défrichement; culture en couloirs (corridor system); matière organique du sol / humus; sol ferrallitique / sol latéritique (NOT 'Ferralsol' or 'Oxisol'); rendement en kg/ha; capacité d'échange de bases. Series to dig: INÉAC Série Scientifique (e.g. Bartholomew, Meyer & Laudelout 1953, mineral nutrient immobilization under forest and grass fallow, Yangambi region), Série Technique, Hors Série (the annual Rapport Annuel volumes, e.g. the 1949 report, 306 pp., publ. 1950), Bulletin d'Information de l'INÉAC (1952–1960), and Jurion & Henry 1969 'Can primitive farming be modernised?' which synthesises the corridor-system rotation trials. Custody: Royal Academy for Overseas Sciences (KAOWARSOM/ARSOM) holds a digitisation inventory (INEAC.xlsx) and states digitised INÉAC publications are 'available at request'; originals and archives at Meise Botanic Garden, the Royal Museum for Central Africa, and the National Archives of Belgium. Also check the Gembloux Agro-Bio Tech library and ORSTOM/IRAT French-colonial analogues (Bambey, Grimari, Boukoko) as a second corpus. TRAPS: (1) Do NOT write that Africa has no LTEs — Saria (Burkina Faso), Kabete and Machang'a (Kenya), Samaru (Nigeria), IITA Ibadan all exist and ARE used; the claim must be narrowed to pre-1960, humid-tropical, Congo-basin Ferralsol, with fallow-length arms. (2) Do NOT re-do the phenology/climate rescue — the INÉAC Yangambi phenology tables (~1937–1956) and the climate record are ALREADY digitised (COBIMFO, Belspo SD/AR/01A) and published; that is the complement, not the target. (3) The real kill risk is not citation but adequacy: if the reports give only station-mean yields with no initial SOC, bulk density or residue-return information, the modelling use collapses — check one Rapport Annuel for plot-level tables BEFORE investing. || CORE PREMISE: The INÉAC 1933–1960 agronomic corpus contains multi-year, treatment-resolved yield and soil-organic-matter series from humid-tropical Congo-basin Ferralsols, including fallow-length arms, and no soil-crop or SOC modelling paper has ever used any of it. || DISCONTINUITY: Congolese independence, 30 June 1960, followed within days by the Force Publique mutiny and the evacuation of INÉAC's Belgian scientific staff from Yangambi; INÉAC was formally wound up in 1962 and its functions passed to INERA. The running experiments were abandoned mid-rotation, the publication series stopped, and the records were physically removed to three separate Belgian institutions (Meise Botanic Garden, Royal Museum for Central Africa, National Archives of Belgium). || GAP MECHANISM: Custody and institutional death, not citation sloth. The institute that owned the plots ceased to exist in 1962, so no successor inherited either the field sites or any obligation to publish the accumulated series; the output format was French-language print monographs in four institute-internal series with no DOIs, absent from Scopus/WoS/CrossRef, held in Belgium and supplied 'at request' rather than web-indexed; and the modern African LTE literature restarted in English in the 1970s–80s on entirely new sites with new protocols, so there is no bibliographic path from a 2024 model-intercomparison paper back to a 1954 Bulletin d'Information. The partial rescues that HAVE happened (phenology, climate) were done by forest-ecology teams who had no reason to touch the agronomy volumes — direct evidence that the archive is tractable and that the agronomic arms were simply left behind. || PREMISES VERIFIED: Searched the modern side and read what the most on-point documents actually say. Couëdel et al. 2024, European Journal of Agronomy, 'Long-term soil organic carbon and crop yield feedbacks differ between 16 soil-crop models in sub-Saharan Africa' (also in the IFDC repository): it uses data from FOUR long-term maize experiments in SSA, and concludes that the results 'highlight the need for long-term experiments in which root and soil N dynamics are monitored' and that such data 'would improve and calibrate soil-crop models'. A companion RothC/Century evaluation on two Kenyan datasets states that 'there are few examples of specific parameterisation of these models for environmental conditions in East Africa'. Searches pairing Yangambi/INÉAC with RothC, DSSAT, SOC-model calibration returned NOTHING on the Congo corpus — only Chinese, German and Kenyan LTEs. On the old side: the KAOWARSOM INÉAC page says only 'The following publications from this institute have been digitised by RAOS and are available at request', with an overview spreadsheet (INEAC.xlsx) and no public listing; the catalogue confirms a Bartholomew/Meyer/Laudelout 1953 Série Scientifique study on mineral nutrient immobilization under forest and grass fallow in the Yangambi region, a 306-page 1949 Rapport Annuel (Hors Série, 1950), and Série Technique no. 19 (1938), i.e. the series exist and contain quantitative fallow work. What I did NOT verify: that any single INÉAC volume prints plot-level treatment × year yields. That is step (a) of the scout's job. || COHERENCE: No physical-regime hazard: this is archive recovery plus model calibration, not a new experiment, and the climate forcing needed to drive the models already exists in digitised form for the same site and years. The arithmetic to check is bookkeeping, not physics: whether reported yields are per-plot or station means, whether soil organic matter is reported as % organic matter (× ~0.58 to get %C, a conversion that must be stated, not assumed) over a stated depth, and whether bulk density is given at all — a %C-only series cannot be converted to Mg C/ha without it, and inventing a bulk density is exactly how a rescue like this produces a spurious SOC trend. Fallow-length arms must be checked for confounding with the corridor system's spatial rotation. || HOW TO CHECK: Falsifiable in two cheap steps. (a) Obtain one INÉAC Rapport Annuel (Hors Série) and one Série Technique volume from KAOWARSOM and check whether yields are reported per treatment per year with soil analyses; if only station means, the target dies immediately. (b) Query OpenAlex/Scopus/Google Scholar for co-citation of 'Yangambi' or 'INÉAC' with RothC / Century / DSSAT / APSIM / 'soil organic carbon model'; my searches returned zero. Success criterion: a digitised treatment × year matrix for at least one fallow-length or continuous-fertiliser arm of ≥8 years, driveable with the existing Yangambi daily weather record.
targets.domain: Agricultural and ecological long-term field experiments still running or archived, whose historical treatment arms answer questions now asked of models

targets.problem: Converting abandoned coal mines into underground reservoirs (UPSH, mine-water storage) puts the roof and ribs above the water line into a forced humidity cycle driven by air displaced through the shafts as the reservoir fills and drains. The most on-point modern review names this as a live degradation mechanism and supports it almost entirely with laboratory specimen cycling. The US Bureau of Mines quantified it in operating mines in the late 1970s and early 1980s and then engineered a mitigation and published design rules for it: Report of Investigations 8955 (Gary P. Sames, USBM Pittsburgh, 1985), 'Coal Mine Air Tempering: Effectiveness, Design, and Roof Support', specifies tempering entries sited as near the main intake as possible with a minimum of 20 to 30 minutes of air residence time, on the finding that most of the effect of specific humidity fluctuations can be concentrated in and absorbed by the tempering entries. Recover that corpus - RI 8291 (1978) on humidity as a cyclic effect in roof stability, Cummings, Moebs and Singh, 'Effect of atmospheric moisture on the deterioration of coal mine roof shales', Mining Engineering 35(3):243-245, March 1983, IC 8976 (1984) summarising the underground and laboratory contract measurements, and RI 8955 (1985) - and hand UPSH and mine-reuse designers a field-calibrated penetration depth, a humidity threshold and an already-engineered ventilation fix for the above-water-line zone.
targets.notes: B-terms and the OLD vocabulary: 'air slacking' (the USBM spelling; modern spelling is 'air slaking'); 'moisture-sensitive shale'; 'deterioration-prone shale'; 'air tempering' and 'tempering panel' / 'tempering entries'; 'specific humidity' (not relative humidity - the old corpus uses the absolute measure, which is the physically correct driver and a genuine vocabulary split); 'air residence time'; 'roof fall rate'; 'intake air'; 'guniting' and 'sealant plan'; 'Dykersburg Shale'; 'Harrisburg (No. 5) Coalbed'; 'Pittsburgh Coalbed'; 'Dunkard Basin'. Where to dig: stacks.cdc.gov holds the scanned USBM RI and IC series and the NIOSH Mining Publications records (RI 8955 is cdc/10356; the Cummings-Moebs-Singh 1983 record is cdc/246546); onemine.org for the SME/AIME side; the annual Conference on Ground Control in Mining proceedings (West Virginia University, 1981 onward). TRAPS, and read these before writing anything: (1) Colas et al. 2023 DOES cite one paper from this lineage by name - '[73] R.A. Cummings, Identification of mine roof susceptibility to air slacking, Int. J. Coal Geol. 8(4), 1987'. Do NOT claim the lineage is uncited. The honest claim is narrower: the review imported the index test that tells you which rock is susceptible, and not the in-mine field quantification (RI 8291, the 1983 Mining Engineering paper) nor the engineered mitigation with its design numbers (RI 8955). State it that way or the target deserves to be killed. (2) NIOSH did not abandon the topic - there is a 2009 SME paper on time-dependent roof deterioration at a central Ohio mine reporting more roof falls in dry winter months, more convergence April-September, and that mine air does not mix with air in roof boreholes. Treat that finding as an asset: it bounds the penetration depth of the humidity cycle. (3) The 1978 RI 8291 details (roof-fall records 1972-1975, sinusoidal fits of one-year period) came to me from a catalogue snippet, not from the report; verify against the scanned report before quoting. || CORE PREMISE: The field quantification of humidity-cycle-driven shale roof deterioration in operating coal mines, and the engineered ventilation mitigation derived from it, exist as specified designs in the 1978-1985 US Bureau of Mines Report of Investigations corpus, and are absent from the modern underground-energy-storage literature that names the same mechanism and proposes no mitigation for it. || DISCONTINUITY: Two dated events, both documented. (a) 15 November 1990: the Clean Air Act Amendments were signed, and utilities serving the high-sulphur Illinois Basin overwhelmingly switched to low-sulphur Powder River Basin coal rather than scrub. Illinois coal production fell from 61.7 million tons in 1990 to 33.5 million tons by 2000 and employment from about 10,000 to under 3,500; the older underground mines in the Harrisburg (No. 5) and Herrin (No. 6) coalbeds - precisely the moisture-sensitive-roof mines of this corpus - closed. The practice of air tempering died with its host mines. (b) March 1996: the US Bureau of Mines was abolished under the FY1996 appropriations act (Pub. L. 104-134); 12 locations were closed and about 1,200 employees terminated in March 1996, with health-and-safety research transferred to NIOSH in FY1997 and the Bureau's numbered Report of Investigations and Information Circular series terminated. The surviving documents sit as scanned PDFs on stacks.cdc.gov without DOIs and outside Scopus and Web of Science. || GAP MECHANISM: Not a citation count. (1) Documented commercial abandonment: the engineering practice (air tempering panels) and the mines it was designed for were eliminated by a single piece of 1990 air-quality legislation, so no practitioner carried the design rules forward. (2) Institutional dissolution plus a publication-channel death: the USBM RI/IC grey-literature series ended in 1996 and the corpus is now undiscoverable through the indexes the modern energy-storage community searches - which is why the one item that did cross over is the single paper from the programme that happened to be published in a journal (Cummings 1987, Int. J. Coal Geol.) rather than in the RI series. (3) Vocabulary and metric split for the same quantity: the old corpus controls on 'specific humidity' of intake air and reports 'roof fall rate'; the modern literature reports strength loss versus 'number of wetting-drying cycles' on specimens. There is no shared independent variable, so the two bodies cannot be compared without translation. || PREMISES VERIFIED: (i) I extracted and read the full text and the 224-entry reference list of the single most on-point modern document: Colas et al., Journal of Energy Storage 73(D):109153, 2023. It has a section 2.2.1 'Humidity changes' which states that wetting of the rock around the cavities after long-term exposure to atmospheric conditions including the ventilation can cause decreasing strength and stiffness, and that slaking is well documented in coal mines and associated with potential roof instabilities; and a section 5.1 'Cyclic wetting and drying' whose support is laboratory specimen work (refs 156-159, plus Opalinus Clay under cyclic relative humidity, ref 71). I read the relevant reference entries individually. Its Bureau of Mines citations are [36] Molinda and Mark, 'Rating the Strength of Coal Mine Roof Rocks', 1996; [127] Ulery and Molinda on methane emissions, RI 1984; [128] Diamond on coalbed gas drainage, 1982 - i.e. roof-rock rating and gas, not the humidity/air-tempering programme. Section 5.1 proposes no mitigation. (ii) I read the stacks.cdc.gov record for RI 8955 directly: title 'Coal Mine Air Tempering: Effectiveness, Design, and Roof Support', Gary P. Sames, 1985, USBM Pittsburgh, specifying 'a minimum of 20- to 30- min air residence time' and that most of the effect of specific humidity fluctuations can be concentrated in and absorbed by the tempering entries. (iii) I read the stacks.cdc.gov record for Cummings, Moebs and Singh, 'Effect of atmospheric moisture on the deterioration of coal mine roof shales', Mining Engineering 35(3):243-245, March 1983, which describes a 2-year Bureau of Mines programme and states that 'Fluctuating moisture conditions are particularly deleterious'. (iv) I verified the Illinois Basin production and employment collapse figures and the 1990 CAAA fuel-switching cause, and the March 1996 USBM closure under Pub. L. 104-134. HONEST WEAKNESS, stated up front: this target is weaker than the Tressange one precisely because the review does cite Cummings 1987 by name. If the scout judges that one citation to mean the bridge is built, kill it fast and say so. || COHERENCE: Checked, and it forces a real scope restriction that the scout must carry. Moisture diffusion penetration depth scales as the square root of the cycle period, so a 24-hour UPSH cycle penetrates about sqrt(365) = 19 times less deep than the annual ventilation-humidity cycle the USBM corpus measured. If the annual cycle affects a skin of order 0.3-1 m of shale roof, a daily cycle affects of order 1.5-5 cm. The USBM data therefore bound the affected skin from ABOVE and speak to the seasonal and multi-day component of reservoir operation, not to hourly turbine cycling - this must be said explicitly or the transfer is overclaimed. Sign is consistent in both literatures: moisture gain and loss weaken the shale. Second scope point: UPSH immerses the lower part of the reservoir in liquid water, which is a different boundary condition; the USBM corpus applies to the above-water-line zone, the freeboard and the ventilation shafts - which is exactly the zone Colas et al. section 2.2.1 identifies. Third, flagged risk: the 20-30 minute residence-time rule was derived for a continuous mine ventilation circuit, whereas UPSH air exchange is a large pulsed volume displaced by the changing water level, so tempering may simply not be achievable at those flow rates. The scout must check the air-volume arithmetic for a representative scheme before recommending the mitigation, and should fall back to the dewpoint-versus-rock-temperature criterion and the penetration-depth data if tempering proves infeasible. || HOW TO CHECK: Moderate to high, and cheap to kill. The documents are specific, numbered and freely readable on stacks.cdc.gov, so the first hour either confirms or destroys the claim. Falsification tests in order: (1) read RI 8291, IC 8976 and RI 8955 in full - if they contain only laboratory index tests and no in-mine humidity-versus-deformation records, the target dies, because then the field quantification never existed; (2) search any post-2018 underground-energy-storage or mine-reuse paper for 'air tempering' - a single hit means the bridge exists; (3) do the air-volume arithmetic above - if tempering is infeasible at UPSH flow rates, the deliverable shrinks from a mitigation design to a field-calibrated penetration depth and humidity threshold, which is still worth having but should be reported as the smaller result rather than dressed up.
targets.domain: Mine, tunnel and quarry rock-mechanics instrumentation from workings now closed

targets.problem: The 2020s literature that characterizes waste-plastic- and tire-derived pyrolysis oils for refinery/steam-cracker reinsertion is re-deriving, one method at a time, the hydrocarbon group-type and distillation measurement biases that the 1974-1986 synthetic-fuels programmes already quantified in MULTI-LABORATORY round robins on coal- and shale-derived liquids. Recover those published interlaboratory transfer functions (FIA/ASTM D1319 vs mass-spectrometric group type vs preparative HPLC; ASTM D86 atmospheric vs D1160 reduced-pressure vs simulated distillation) together with their measured bias magnitudes, signs and reproducibility limits, and test whether they predict the discrepancies now being reported on aromatic/heteroatom-rich pyrolysis oils. If they do, the pyrolysis-oil community can adopt an existing bias-and-precision prior for its emerging specifications instead of spending another decade re-measuring it.
targets.notes:
B-TERMS: fluorescent indicator adsorption (FIA, ASTM D1319); hydrocarbon group type / PONA / PIONA; mass-spectrometric group type (D2425, D2786, D3239); preparative/HPLC group separation with RI detection; bromine number and olefin determination; basic nitrogen; tar acids/phenolics; simulated distillation (D2887/D7500) vs physical distillation (D86/D1160).
OLD VOCABULARY to search INSTEAD of modern words: 'syncrude', 'coal syncrude', 'coal liquid', 'SRC-I'/'SRC-II' (Solvent Refined Coal), 'H-Coal', 'EDS' (Exxon Donor Solvent), 'Synthoil', 'shale oil', 'retorted shale oil', 'Paraho', 'TOSCO II', 'alternate fuels', 'alternative hydrocarbon fuels', 'non-petroleum derived fuels', 'shale-derived JP-5/JP-8'. Searching 'pyrolysis oil', 'circular feedstock' or 'chemically recycled naphtha' will never reach this corpus.
WHERE TO DIG: OSTI.gov and NTIS (DOE/PC, DOE/ET, FE report series); ACS Division of Fuel Chemistry preprints; Advances in Chemistry Series 179 'Refining of Synthetic Crudes' (1979); NASA NTRS (Lewis Research Center alternate-fuels work, Antoine and co-workers); ASTM Committee D02 research reports and STPs; Analytical Chemistry and Fuel 1976-1986; AFAPL/AFWAL Wright-Patterson reports on shale-derived JP fuels; Laramie and Bartlesville Energy Technology Center report series.
TRAPS TO AVOID: (a) do NOT write that nobody ever compared pyrolysis oil to coal liquids - Maggi & Delmon did it for biomass bio-oil; the claim is specific to waste-plastic and tire oils. (b) Do NOT claim the method limitations are unknown; ASTM already warns. The asset is the number, not the warning. (c) Do NOT extend the bridge to clean polyolefin (PE/PP) naphtha, which is paraffinic/olefinic and compositionally unlike coal liquids. (d) Do NOT treat GC x GC as the old reference method; the old reference was mass-spec group type or preparative separation, so the comparison chain is old-FIA-vs-old-MS against new-FIA-vs-GCxGC, and the comparability of the two REFERENCE methods must itself be established before any bias number is transferred. (e) The modern finding that FIA 'reports some dienes and heterocompounds as aromatics' points at the olefinic SHALE-oil corpus more than the hydrogen-poor coal corpus; split the search between the two donor literatures accordingly. || CORE PREMISE: The paired-method, multi-laboratory group-type and distillation bias determinations made on coal- and shale-derived liquids c. 1974-1986 are neither cited nor reused by the current plastic/tire pyrolysis-oil characterization literature, even though that literature is independently re-measuring the same method artifacts on compositionally analogous non-petroleum liquids. ATTACK I RAN ON IT MYSELF: the obvious killer is that someone already bridged synfuel liquids to pyrolysis oils, and partly someone did - Maggi & Delmon (OSTI 199285, mid-1990s) explicitly compared BIOMASS pyrolysis oils with coal-derived liquids. That bridge exists for bio-oil and is excluded from the claim. The second attack is that the knowledge is not lost because ASTM scope statements still warn about coal/shale/tar-sand products; but a scope warning carries the existence of the problem, not the measured magnitude, sign or reproducibility of the bias, which is the recoverable asset. || DISCONTINUITY: The US Synthetic Fuels Corporation, created by the Energy Security Act of 30 June 1980, was defunded by Congress in December 1985 and terminated in April 1986, ending the programme under which this analytical-methods work was a deliverable. Two flanking dated events bracket it: Exxon cancelled the Colony Shale Oil Project on 2 May 1982 ('Black Sunday'), collapsing the shale-oil analytical community; and DOE's direct coal liquefaction programme wound down with the closure of the Advanced Coal Liquefaction R&D Facility at Wilsonville, Alabama (reported 1992 - a scout should confirm this date at source). The host laboratories were reorganized out of existence or identity: Bartlesville Energy Technology Center became NIPER and lost DOE support; Pittsburgh Energy Technology Center was absorbed into NETL. || GAP MECHANISM: Not a citation-count gap. Three mechanisms compound. (1) VENUE: the work was programme deliverable literature - DOE/NTIS grey reports, ACS Division of Fuel Chemistry preprints, a NASA conference paper, ASTM D02 research reports - almost none of it in indexed, DOI-bearing journals, and much of it only as page scans without OCR (the key 1977 NASA item is an un-OCRed scan, which is why my own attempt to read its numbers failed). (2) VOCABULARY SPLIT FOR THE SAME PHYSICAL OBJECT: the identical analyte class - a non-petroleum, heteroatom- and unsaturate-rich liquid being forced through petroleum test methods - is called 'syncrude'/'coal liquid'/'shale oil' in the donor literature and 'pyrolysis oil'/'chemically recycled feedstock' in the recipient literature, with no shared keyword. (3) SCOPE CONDITION FROZEN INTO THE STANDARD: ASTM method scopes preserve the warning that applicability to coal, shale and tar-sand products was never determined, which tells modern users a problem exists while pointing nowhere, so the natural next step is to re-measure rather than to go looking. || PREMISES VERIFIED: WHAT I ACTUALLY READ, not snippets. (1) Via Crossref API I retrieved and read the full structured reference list of the single most on-point modern document: 'A comparative study of aromatic content in pyrolysis oils from waste plastics and tires: Assessing common refinery methods', Fuel 2024, DOI 10.1016/j.fuel.2024.131714. It has 36 references. Oldest is 1984. Only three predate 1995 (1984, 1985, 1994). ZERO reference titles contain coal, shale, syncrude or synfuel. One 2014 title contains 'Synthetic Fuels' - 'Hydrocarbon Group-Type Analysis of Petroleum-Derived and Synthetic Fuels Using Two-Dimensional Gas Chromatography' - but it is a modern GC x GC paper, not the synfuel-era corpus. (2) That paper's own findings, as quoted in its abstract: 'HPLC-RI and FIA resulted in significant errors... the FIA reports some dienes and heterocompounds as aromatics... monoaromatics are overestimated, while polyaromatics are underestimated. Among the tested methods, GC x GC-FID provided the most reliable results.' (3) OLD CORPUS ANCHOR CONFIRMED AT SOURCE RECORD: NASA NTRS records 19780005290 and 19780040997, Albert C. Antoine (NASA Lewis Research Center), 'Hydrocarbon Group Type Determination in Jet Fuels by High Performance Liquid Chromatography', FACSS IV, Detroit, 7-11 November 1977. Thirty-two jet and diesel samples prepared from oil shale and coal syncrudes, plus two petroleum Jet A controls; hydrocarbon types by FIA with 'results from three laboratories are presented and compared'; two HPLC methods also compared. I confirmed the record and its front matter. I could NOT read the numbers: the PDF is an un-OCRed 3.4 MB scan and no page-rendering tool was available in this environment. So the EXISTENCE and SHAPE of a three-laboratory FIA intercomparison on coal/shale syncrude fuels is verified; its numeric content is not. (4) NOT VERIFIED AT SOURCE, flagged: the ASTM D1319 scope sentence that its 'applicability to coal, shale, or tar sand products has not been determined' and that its precision statement may not apply to them appeared only in a search excerpt of a third-party reproduction; astm.org returned HTTP 403. A scout must confirm this from the standard itself before quoting it. (5) NEGATIVE RESULT I recorded against myself: pairing 'pyrolysis oil' with 'coal liquids' surfaces Maggi & Delmon (OSTI 199285) comparing biomass bio-oils with coal-derived liquids, which is why the claim is scoped to plastic/tire oils only. || COHERENCE: Scoped, not assumed. COMPOSITION: coal-derived liquids are hydrogen-poor, highly aromatic, phenol- and basic-nitrogen-rich; retorted shale oil is olefinic and nitrogen-rich; polyolefin (PE/PP) pyrolysis oil is paraffinic/olefinic with low heteroatom content. The transfer therefore applies to the aromatic/heteroatom-rich recipients - tire-derived oil, polystyrene-derived oil, mixed-waste oil containing PET, PVC or polyamide - and, for the olefin/diene interference question specifically, to the shale-oil donor corpus. It does NOT apply to clean polyolefin naphtha, and the target must not be stretched there. REGIME: every method at issue operates in the same boiling and temperature window for both liquid classes - D1319 FIA on fractions distilling below 589 K, HPLC-RI at ambient, D86 at atmospheric pressure, D1160 at reduced pressure, D2887/D7500 simulated distillation - so there is no pressure or temperature incoherence between donor and recipient. SIGN: the bias runs the same direction in both literatures - non-aromatic unsaturates and heteroatom-bearing compounds are counted into the aromatic band, inflating aromatics and distorting the mono/poly split - so the bridge does not require the opposite sign of the effect. || HOW TO CHECK: Cheap and decisive, in three steps. (1) Harvest the 1974-1986 DOE/NTIS, ACS Fuel Chemistry, NASA and ASTM D02 corpus on paired group-type and distillation method comparison for coal and shale liquids; extract the published method-vs-method values and any stated interlaboratory repeatability/reproducibility. The Antoine 1977 three-laboratory FIA/HPLC dataset is the designated first retrieval and will need OCR. (2) Compare the extracted bias magnitudes and signs against the measured FIA and HPLC-RI deviations from GC x GC-FID reported for tire and mixed-plastic oils in Fuel 2024 (10.1016/j.fuel.2024.131714) and in the GC x GC cracker-reintegration studies. (3) PASS if the old biases reproduce the modern discrepancies in sign and within the old interlaboratory reproducibility band, which would let the pyrolysis-oil community import a ready-made bias correction and precision estimate. FALSIFIED if the old corpus contains only single-laboratory applicability notes with no paired-method numbers, or if the extracted bias differs in sign from the modern measurements. Either outcome is reached by document retrieval plus arithmetic - no new experiment required.
targets.domain: Calibration and intercomparison exercises between laboratories, instruments or nations that established transfer functions nobody now reuses

_GENERATION_RULE_added_2026_10_20: MANDATORY for any run that generates new targets. In the 2026-10-20 run, 12 of 21 combed targets carried a FALSE premise written in at generation time: a wrong nobody-has-measured-this, a wrong these-literatures-never-cite-each-other, or (sulfate-below-gypsum) a misquote of the targets own verified-live source. Before appending a target: (1) run the co-occurrence check yourself on the bare concept against the bare target system, with no application-domain words; (2) read the reference list of the single most on-point modern document and confirm the claimed-missing citations really are missing; (3) never write verified live from a search snippet - extract the cited document; (4) prefer targets where the gap is a chemical, physical or mathematical impossibility of the current approach over targets where the gap is merely bibliographic, because every decisive kill in that run came from the former. Also keep the three scout instructions used in batches 4-7 (source fidelity, broad co-occurrence, check-the-premises-first); they measurably improved scout behaviour.
